cases.title: Abrupt visual loss after intraocular lens exchange
cases.task_type: Abrupt visual loss after intraocular lens exchange
cases.summary: A 40-year-old woman undergoes left intraocular lens exchange for recurrent vitreous haemorrhage attributed to uveitis–glaucoma–hyphaema syndrome. She previously had congenital cataract surgery with pars plana vitrectomy, lensectomy and posterior capsulotomy at age 13. Preoperative visual acuity was 20/30 in the left eye and 20/20 in the right. A sulcus single-piece lens has been replaced by a three-piece lens in a reportedly uncomplicated 15-minute procedure. Topical and intracameral agents included lidocaine and phenylephrine; the full medication record is available for review. About ten minutes later she reports complete left-eye visual loss. At thirty minutes she has no light perception and a marked relative afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressure is 8 mm Hg; the cornea is clear. Dilated examination describes an attached, perfused retina without visible detachment, choroidal haemorrhage, optic nerve pallor or vascular occlusion. She has mild ipsilateral supraorbital headache and no reported migraine or neurological history. Neuroimaging has been ordered, but no result is available.
cases.purpose: Write 180–240 words for an ophthalmic clinician. Summarise the urgent problem, compare the important explanations and justify the next assessment priorities. Explain what the apparently preserved retinal appearance does and does not establish. Integrate the operative history and drug exposure without prematurely declaring a benign drug effect. prepared_template.title: Worsening renal function after first-cycle cancer treatment
prepared_template.facts:
Background
A woman in her 40s has newly diagnosed T4N1M1 grade 3 clear cell renal carcinoma. CT shows a right renal mass measuring 20.4 × 12.2 × 13.6 cm, replacing the kidney, invading the liver, with retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, pulmonary metastases and inferior vena cava tumour thrombus with venous congestion. Before treatment, creatinine was 102–116 micromol/L and eGFR 44–51 mL/min/1.73 m². Graves' disease was treated by total thyroidectomy, leaving hypothyroidism and hypoparathyroidism. She previously presented with symptomatic hypercalcaemia.

Treatment and deterioration
Oral lenvatinib and intravenous pembrolizumab were started. Seven days later she presented with persistent vomiting, severe malaise, fatigue and acute kidney injury. There were no focal localising signs of infection. Raised inflammatory markers led to empirical intravenous antibiotics and fluids. Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg was started for suspected treatment-related interstitial nephritis. Metabolic abnormalities persisted and phosphate continued to rise. Urate was not measured during the first three days of this acute presentation. Potassium is described as raised, but its numerical value is not reproduced in the available narrative. LDH was not recorded at presentation. Exact collection times and proof that these values came from the same draw are not supplied.

Current information boundary
No subsequent treatment response, dialysis outcome or cancer-treatment rechallenge is supplied. Current potassium, ECG, urine-output trend, fluid balance, current calcium symptoms and the patient's usual calcium-replacement regimen are not provided.

prepared_template.title: Multiorgan injury with biomarkers peaking at different times
prepared_template.facts:
A previously healthy man in his early 40s, a law-enforcement officer with no prior comorbidities, no smoking or alcohol use, regular exercise and no medications, was brought to an emergency department in central Brazil during a special operations selection course involving strenuous physical activity under deliberate water restriction. During the training he developed nausea, vomiting, syncope and mental confusion.

On initial assessment he was unconscious with a decreased level of consciousness, hypertensive, tachycardic, with an irregular cardiac rhythm, severely dehydrated, afebrile and in an extremely critical overall condition. Respiratory distress with accessory muscle use prompted immediate orotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation.

Physical examination revealed diffuse and extensive haematomas over the chest, abdomen, upper and lower extremities, back, flanks and buttocks, with multiple linear bruising patterns. The severity and distribution of the soft tissue injuries were recorded as disproportionate to what would be expected from exertional injury alone. After extubation and clinical recovery, the patient confirmed that all injuries had been sustained during the training course, with no independent trauma outside the training.

Due to clinical instability and a false-positive rapid antigen test for SARS-CoV-2 (later confirmed negative by RT-PCR), the patient was transferred through two hospitals within the first 24 hours before arriving at a tertiary cardiac care centre, where the severity of organ dysfunction on arrival required mechanical ventilation and emergency haemodialysis.

Key dated laboratory values: potassium 7.3 mmol/L on admission, with hypokalaemia later (nadir 3.1 mmol/L on day 15); creatine kinase peaking at 109 460 U/L; serum myoglobin 7874 ng/mL on day 2; creatinine peaking at 10.41 mg/dL on day 3; lactate dehydrogenase peak 9830 U/L on day 1; high-sensitivity troponin I rising progressively to a delayed peak of 771.9 ng/L on day 20, temporally dissociated from the peaks of CK and myoglobin.

Further acute-phase biochemistry: severe metabolic acidosis with profound respiratory compensation on admission (HCO3− nadir 9.4 mmol/L, base excess −13.2 mmol/L, pH 7.35, PCO2 17.3 mmHg on day 0), followed by overt acidaemia (pH 7.2) on day 1 once mechanical ventilation was initiated; hepatic injury (ALT 1220 U/L, AST 2353 U/L); hyperphosphataemia; hyperuricaemia; pancreatic involvement (amylase peaking at 358 U/L on day 8). Platelet counts remained normal throughout (nadir 221×10⁹/L on day 3) with reactive thrombocytosis thereafter (peak 630×10⁹/L on day 19), and coagulation studies showed no evidence of disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Calcium showed a biphasic pattern: profound hypocalcaemia on admission (ionised calcium nadir 0.61 mmol/L on day 1) followed by rebound hypercalcaemia (peak 1.66 mmol/L by day 16). C-reactive protein showed a bimodal in-hospital pattern with peaks of 182 mg/L on day 2 and 157 mg/L on day 17.

A 12-lead ECG on admission showed sinus rhythm at 71 beats/min with tall, peaked, symmetrical T waves in leads V2–V4, consistent with severe hyperkalaemia. There were no ST-segment changes suggestive of acute coronary syndrome.

Chest radiograph and chest CT on day 1 showed a cardiac silhouette at the upper limit of normal, prominent pulmonary hila, bilateral interstitial infiltrates and areas of consolidation with air bronchograms in the lower lobes bilaterally, predominantly on the left, consistent with bronchopneumonia; scattered ground-glass opacities of non-specific aetiology were noted, and the findings were not consistent with COVID-19 pneumonia. CT of the abdomen (day 1) was unremarkable, excluding solid organ injury despite the extent of external trauma. CT of the brain (day 1) was normal. Arterial blood gas analysis documented recurrent hypoxaemia on supplemental oxygen (PaO2 52.9 mmHg with SaO2 88% on day 7; PaO2 54.4 mmHg with SaO2 90.2% on day 20).

Transthoracic echocardiography on day 9 showed preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (69.3%, Teichholz method) with normal segmental wall motion; speckle-tracking analysis revealed a mildly reduced global longitudinal strain (−16.5%), indicating subclinical myocardial injury despite preserved systolic function. Mild concentric left ventricular hypertrophy was present (interventricular septum and posterior wall 13 mm; indexed left ventricular mass 126.8 g/m²), with significant left atrial enlargement (indexed volume 56 mL/m²), mild right atrial enlargement (39 mL/m²) and grade I diastolic dysfunction. Estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure was 32 mmHg. No pericardial effusion was detected. RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 was negative.

Documented working diagnostic framing during the acute admission: the constellation of massive CK elevation, myoglobinuria, AKI and multi-organ injury in the context of extreme physical exertion under water restriction was recorded as diagnostic of severe exertional rhabdomyolysis. Heatstroke was considered less likely because the patient was afebrile at presentation and core body temperature was not documented as elevated. The extensive pattern of haematomas with multiple linear bruising patterns strongly suggested a traumatic component superimposed on exertional muscle damage.

Treatment during the first admission: orotracheal intubation with mechanical ventilation; a triple-lumen catheter in the right internal jugular vein under ultrasound guidance for emergency haemodialysis; aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation with correction of electrolyte derangements. Haemodialysis was continued throughout the first admission (10 days) and for three additional outpatient sessions. The patient was extubated approximately 48 hours after the initial intubation. Antihypertensive therapy was initiated for secondary hypertension. Intravenous antibiotics were administered for bronchopneumonia confirmed on chest CT.

Recorded data limitations relevant to this review: core body temperature was not documented at presentation (although the patient was afebrile); no prior echocardiogram exists, so structural findings cannot be attributed to the acute event; muscle biopsy and genetic testing were unavailable. This is a constructed selected-record review: the source reports serial data acquired at different times, and the day-20 review point is imposed on data recorded across days 0–20; no pretreatment baseline measurements are supplied.

cases.title: Progressive bilateral visual loss with immunodeficiency and discordant tests
cases.summary:
Background and course
A woman in her 40s has common variable immunodeficiency diagnosed five years earlier, granulomatous-lymphocytic interstitial lung disease, immune-mediated thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly and generalised lymphadenopathy. She receives weekly intravenous immunoglobulin and prophylactic azithromycin three times weekly. Several weeks of painless bilateral blurred vision progressed over days. No specific occupational or home toxic/infective exposure was identified.
cases.purpose: Immunodeficiency and replacement immunoglobulin complicate serology. Treating inflammation also creates infection risk; normal imaging does not settle the mechanism.
cases.source_note: The source combines baseline and three-month MRI reporting. This is explicitly a constructed work-up review, not a reconstructed pre-treatment clock time. Positive serologies are given without the authors’ false-positive interpretation; electrophysiological artefact and non-diagnostic imaging are retained.

prepared_template.title: Progressive bilateral visual loss with immunodeficiency and discordant tests
prepared_template.facts:
Background and course
A woman in her 40s has common variable immunodeficiency diagnosed five years earlier, granulomatous-lymphocytic interstitial lung disease, immune-mediated thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly and generalised lymphadenopathy. She receives weekly intravenous immunoglobulin and prophylactic azithromycin three times weekly. Several weeks of painless bilateral blurred vision progressed over days. No specific occupational or home toxic/infective exposure was identified.

Eye and neurological findings
Visual acuity is 3/60 in each eye; an examination four years previously recorded 6/9 in the right and 6/12 in the left. There are large central scotomas, markedly impaired colour vision, a left relative afferent pupillary defect, sluggish light responses and light–near dissociation. Intraocular pressures are normal and the anterior segments are quiet. Both optic discs are swollen, with grade 1+ vitreous cells. OCT confirms disc swelling with mildly reduced macular ganglion-cell thickness. There is no macular oedema or retinal vasculitis. No other neurological findings are reported.

Laboratory evidence
ESR is 82 mm/hour, ACE 79 U/L, soluble interleukin-2 receptor exceeds 10,000 ng/L, and CRP is 5 mg/L. Thrombocytopenia is stable. Culture, molecular and antigen-based tests for the reported viral, tuberculosis, toxoplasma and bartonella investigations are negative. Treponemal antibody is positive with a normal rapid plasma reagin result; Borrelia IgG is positive and IgM negative. Aquaporin-4, MOG and antiphospholipid antibody screens are negative. Folate, B12 and thyroid testing are normal.

Imaging, CSF and electrophysiology
The available contrast MRI account of brain, orbits and spine describes no compressive/infiltrative lesion or remote white-matter/cord lesions typical of MS or neuromyelitis optica, and no definite optic-nerve enhancement. CT venography shows no venous sinus thrombosis. PET-CT shows the known lymphadenopathy and non-FDG-avid pulmonary nodules. CSF opening pressure and routine constituents are normal. Full-field ERG is normal. Pattern ERG has reduced P50 amplitudes and an early P50 peak; N95 cannot be assessed reliably because of movement-related baseline drift. Pattern visual evoked potentials are present but poorly formed, preventing reliable quantification; flash responses are simplified.

Timing limits
The publication groups initial and repeat MRI findings three months apart. This packet supplies the selected diagnostic findings together; it does not establish the exact order of all tests, their timing relative to IVIg infusions, or which results preceded initial treatment. Interim treatment exposure and response are not provided.

cases.title: Fever, anaemia and graft dysfunction despite a rejection-directed treatment
cases.summary:
Transplant background
A woman in her 60s received a kidney transplant for adult polycystic kidney disease one year and ten months earlier. The donor had previous CMV/EBV infection; the recipient was CMV IgG negative and EBV IgG positive. Induction used basiliximab and methylprednisolone. Maintenance used tacrolimus and mycophenolate; prednisolone stopped at six weeks. Five months before this presentation, mycophenolate mofetil 750 mg twice daily was changed to mycophenolic acid 180 mg twice daily. Tacrolimus levels previously around 7 micrograms/L fell to approximately 3–4 during the preceding three months.
cases.purpose: A positive graft-biopsy finding may be contributory without explaining the whole illness. Negative circulating viral tests do not resolve every malignancy question.
cases.source_note: The biopsy finding and minimal steroid response are retained without labelling rejection false. Negative serum EBV is an observed result, not an exclusion criterion supplied to the model. Later response is not used to prove what caused the graft dysfunction.

A woman in her 60s received a kidney transplant for adult polycystic kidney disease one year and ten months earlier. Prior infections and current illness
She had recurrent C. difficile infection and an episode of CMV disease at approximately 18 months post-transplant, with diarrhoea and electrolyte disturbance. She now has fever, loss of appetite, fatigue, generalised weakness, pallor and reduced mobility. Systemic examination is otherwise unrevealing. Anaemia present for two to three months has worsened. Creatinine is 308 micromol/L, compared with baseline 175; CRP is 104 mg/L. Bilirubin and liver tests are normal.

Infection and imaging results
Blood, urine, sputum and stool cultures and serum CMV, EBV and BK viral loads are negative. Procalcitonin is 2.1 micrograms/L. CT and graft MRI show no deep infection or obstruction; the graft appears well perfused. The spleen measures 22 cm.

Biopsy and response
Graft biopsy contains 22 glomeruli, two obsolete, borderline acute T-cell-mediated rejection, moderate arteriolar hyalinosis and 5% tubular atrophy. No diagnostic intravascular abnormal lymphoid infiltrate is identified in that sample. Three doses of intravenous methylprednisolone 500 mg produce minimal improvement in graft function.

Haematology findings now available
Iron levels are low and two intravenous iron doses have been given. Laboratory results do not show haemolysis. The blood film contains an atypical monomorphic population of small-to-medium lymphoid cells. Peripheral blood flow cytometry confirms a monoclonal B-cell population. The exact current haemoglobin, marrow result, subtype classification and staging are not yet supplied.

cases.title: A preterm infant with major perioperative blood-pressure changes and new brain abnormalities
cases.summary:
Before birth and early neonatal course
At 29 weeks, a pregnancy complicated by severe polyhydramnios and membrane rupture was found to have a large fetal right renal mass compressing abdominal organs. Antenatal steroids, antibiotics and magnesium sulfate were given. A male infant was born at 30 weeks, weighing 1.6 kg, with Apgar scores of 6 and 9. Poor breathing required intubation and surfactant. He was extubated to non-invasive support on day 3, re-intubated on day 5 for surgery, and remained in neonatal intensive care throughout. No chorioamnionitis is reported.
cases.purpose: Prematurity, pressure changes, surgery and incomplete monitoring overlap. A temporal sequence does not establish one exclusive cause of brain injury.
cases.source_note: Life-day and postoperative-day clocks are retained separately. A conflicting reported mean pressure is explicitly flagged rather than silently recalculated or used as an established value. The ultrasound evolution is available, but its single cause is not stipulated.

prepared_template.facts:
Before birth and early neonatal course
At 29 weeks, a pregnancy complicated by severe polyhydramnios and membrane rupture was found to have a large fetal right renal mass compressing abdominal organs. Antenatal steroids, antibiotics and magnesium sulfate were given. A male infant was born at 30 weeks, weighing 1.6 kg, with Apgar scores of 6 and 9. Poor breathing required intubation and surfactant. He was extubated to non-invasive support on day 3, re-intubated on day 5 for surgery, and remained in neonatal intensive care throughout. No chorioamnionitis is reported.

Preoperative findings
Systolic blood pressure was usually 100–110 mmHg and peaked at 141/70. Hydralazine provided temporary control. Renin exceeded 500 mIU/L (reference 4.4–46.1) and aldosterone was 18,391 pmol/L (reference 524–3890). Day-1 ultrasound showed an intrarenal mass 6.4 × 4.2 × 5.4 cm; day-4 CT showed a 7.2 × 5.4 × 6.1 cm mass with a perirenal haematoma and displacement of the inferior vena cava. Urinary HVA/creatinine and VMA/creatinine ratios were within the stated reference ranges. Initial cranial ultrasound was normal. Echocardiography showed mild LV hypertrophy with preserved systolic function. Other antihypertensives were considered but not administered before surgery.

Surgery and circulation
Right radical nephrectomy and partial ureterectomy occurred on day 6 of life. Preoperatively he received packed red cells 15 mL/kg. An arterial line was inserted. No intraoperative hypotension was recorded; an anticipatory saline bolus of 10 mL/kg was given. Sudden hypotension followed surgery. Three further saline boluses of 10 mL/kg gave temporary improvement. During the next 24 hours the recorded BP nadir was 30/15 mmHg and urine output fell below 0.5 mL/kg/hour. Epinephrine and norepinephrine were used. The arterial line was removed because the hand became discoloured; replacement failed, so invasive BP monitoring was not continuous. Hydrocortisone was given for refractory hypotension and blood pressure stabilised over three days.

Respiratory and brain course
One postoperative PCO2 measurement exceeded 9.2 kPa and improved after ventilator adjustment; no hypocapnia was documented. He was extubated on postoperative day 4, on CPAP on day 5, and in room air with saturations above 95% from day 6. One week postoperatively, cranial ultrasound showed new symmetric periventricular echogenicity without cysts. By the second postoperative week, bilateral frontoparietal white-matter cystic changes were present. Postoperative renal pathology reported a mixed-type congenital mesoblastic nephroma; the exact pathology reporting date is not supplied.

Record limits
The source pairs BP 30/15 with a stated mean pressure of 26 mmHg; their correspondence is not resolved. A continuous perioperative BP trace and full timing of blood gases, oxygenation and cerebral perfusion are not supplied. Term-corrected development is not supplied.

cases.title: A new central neurological pattern during recovery from an areflexic weakness syndrome
cases.summary:
Initial admission
A woman in her 30s developed left-arm weakness progressing to quadriparesis within 24 hours, with neck and respiratory-muscle weakness, absent reflexes, no sensory symptoms, and no bowel/bladder or cranial-nerve involvement. BP was 122/86 and pulse 86. There was no preceding fever, diarrhoea, vaccination or trauma. A provisional clinical diagnosis of Guillain–Barré syndrome was made. Day-1 CSF had 2 lymphocytes/microlitre, protein 44 mg/dL and glucose 62 mg/dL. A ganglioside antibody panel was negative.

prepared_template.title: A new central neurological pattern during recovery from an areflexic weakness syndrome
prepared_template.facts:
Initial admission
A woman in her 30s developed left-arm weakness progressing to quadriparesis within 24 hours, with neck and respiratory-muscle weakness, absent reflexes, no sensory symptoms, and no bowel/bladder or cranial-nerve involvement. BP was 122/86 and pulse 86. There was no preceding fever, diarrhoea, vaccination or trauma. A provisional clinical diagnosis of Guillain–Barré syndrome was made. Day-1 CSF had 2 lymphocytes/microlitre, protein 44 mg/dL and glucose 62 mg/dL. A ganglioside antibody panel was negative.

Early electrophysiology and treatment
Day-2 studies showed absent H-reflexes and prolonged F-wave latencies. Median/ulnar CMAPs were 4–6 mV and tibial/peroneal CMAPs 2–3 mV. Median/ulnar SNAPs were 5–8 microvolts and sural SNAPs 10–12. Distal latencies and velocities were normal, without block or temporal dispersion. The study did not establish a definite axonal or demyelinating subtype. Two plasma exchanges, 48 hours apart at approximately 3,200 mL each, were stopped for haemodynamic intolerance. After stabilisation, IVIg 2 g/kg was given over five days. Weakness stopped progressing but normal strength did not return. She did not need assisted ventilation and transferred to rehabilitation on day 23.

New illness at readmission
Approximately one week later, on day 31, the right leg abruptly worsened. BP was 200/120 and pulse 118. Right distal-leg strength was now 0/5; other severe weakness persisted. Left-leg reflexes were now brisk and the left plantar response was extensor, whereas reflexes had previously been absent. There was no reported thunderclap headache, papilloedema, neck stiffness or new cranial-nerve finding.

New investigations
MRI showed acute infarcts in distal anterior-cerebral-artery territories in both parasagittal frontoparietal regions and the posterior corpus-callosum body, with smaller acute right-cerebellar infarcts and diffuse leptomeningeal/sulcal enhancement. MRA showed irregular multifocal narrowing in the anterior and posterior intracranial circulation. CSF on day 31, 22 days after IVIg completion, had 7 cells/microlitre, protein 56 mg/dL (reference 15–45) and glucose 64 mg/dL. HSV/VZV PCR, tuberculosis and cryptococcal studies, and bacterial/fungal cultures were negative. ANA and ANCA were negative and ACE normal.

What is not established
No catheter angiography, vessel-wall imaging, histopathology or follow-up demonstration of vascular reversibility is available. No subsequent treatment response or clinical outcome is provided.

prepared_template.facts:
A 17-year-old female with juvenile dermatomyositis, avoidant restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID), generalised anxiety disorder, ADHD and a complex psychosocial background was admitted with persistent nausea, food refusal and refusal to speak over the past 2 months.

She lived with her father, who was not available at admission; her mother was deceased. The initial history was primarily provided by her grandmother, who had supported her growing medical needs over the past month.

She had consumed only water and tea and had lost 5 kg over the past month, attributed to nausea, vomiting and food aversion. Her grandmother reported increasing social withdrawal and poor communication.

Her juvenile dermatomyositis was diagnosed at age 11 with proximal muscle weakness and violaceous plaques, in remission on intravenous immune globulin prescribed by her paediatric rheumatologist. She was followed by adolescent medicine for atypical restricting-type anorexia nervosa with fluctuating weight, and had lost 19 kg over the 10 months preceding admission. Anxiety and ADHD were managed by a psychologist and adolescent medicine physician.

On admission she appeared cachectic, dishevelled and minimally responsive, communicating by gestures, head nods or writing, with new urinary incontinence. Initial vital signs demonstrated tachycardia.

She initially refused an oral examination due to fear of emesis; a later limited inspection revealed poor dentition. Cardiac examination showed tachycardia without murmurs, rubs or gallops. Pulmonary, abdominal and dermatological examinations were normal, without lanugo. Extremities were warm and well-perfused with no muscle tenderness or arthritis and negative Russell's sign.

Neurological examination: she could open eyes on command, had full extraocular movements with horizontal end-gaze nystagmus, and absent patellar reflexes.

Emergency department laboratory results obtained prior to fluid resuscitation: lipase 219 U/L; sodium 151 mmol/L; potassium 3.3 mmol/L; blood urea nitrogen 33 mg/dL; creatinine 0.88 mg/dL (increased from 0.57 mg/dL 2 weeks prior); aspartate aminotransferase 33 U/L; alanine aminotransferase 59 U/L.

Complete blood count: normal leucocyte count and haemoglobin; MCV 73 fL; MCHC 302 g/L; RDW 24.8%; platelets elevated at 668 × 10⁹/L. Urine pregnancy test negative. Serum acetaminophen, salicylate and alcohol levels undetectable; urine drug screen negative.

Availability limits: this is a constructed selected-record review. Data recorded here were acquired at different times — admission history and examination, emergency department bloods before fluid resuscitation, and a creatinine measured 2 weeks before admission. No brain imaging, vitamin levels, toxicology beyond the screens above, rheumatological serology, lumbar puncture or nutritional studies are documented at this assessment point; their results are not available and must not be assumed normal. No treatment decisions after admission are recorded here.

Proposed candidate information requirements (unconfirmed candidates, not validated clinical truth, and not documented decisions): (1) Urgent brain MRI, or clinically equivalent urgent neuroimaging plus neurology review, to characterise the encephalopathic picture and nystagmus — justified by altered responsiveness with neurological signs in severe malnutrition; timing: within hours, but proposed imaging must not delay protective treatment. (2) Corroborating collateral history and prior records — from the father when reachable, the grandmother, her paediatric rheumatologist and adolescent medicine physician — covering exact intake, medications, prior weights and psychiatric history; timing: within the first hospital day, as it may discriminate physical illness from behavioural explanations and inform safe feeding.

prepared_template.title: Cardiac dysfunction with retroperitoneal and skeletal abnormalities
prepared_template.facts:
A man in his 30s presented with 3 weeks of pleuritic chest discomfort, progressive exertional dyspnoea, a 20-lb weight gain and diffuse swelling of the lower extremities, abdomen and scrotum. He had a remote diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis at age 10 years involving the sphenoid sinus and turbinate, treated with vinblastine and prednisone, in remission since. He was not taking any medication.

He reported no recent sore throat, cough, chest injury, presyncope, syncope, orthopnoea, focal neurologic deficits, travel or sick contacts. Family history was negative for histiocytosis. Cardiovascular risk factors included severe obesity (body mass index 37 kg/m²) and a father with coronary artery disease at an advanced age. HbA1c and a lipid profile were not obtained during this admission.

On arrival he was afebrile and alert, heart rate in the 110s, respiratory rate in the 20s, blood pressure 158/82 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Examination showed a regular rhythm with distant heart sounds, rhonchi at both lung bases, 3+ pitting oedema to thigh level and a grossly swollen scrotum. Jugular venous distension could not be assessed due to body habitus.

Initial bloods showed microcytic anaemia (haemoglobin 88 g/L, haematocrit 0.281 L/L), leucocytosis (WBC 12×10⁹/L, neutrophil dominant) and thrombocytosis (platelets 471×10⁹/L). Troponins, comprehensive metabolic panel, urinalysis, urine protein and thyroid-stimulating hormone were within normal range.

Chest radiography showed cardiomegaly with pulmonary oedema and small pleural effusions. ECG showed sinus tachycardia at 102 bpm but was otherwise normal.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a large pericardial effusion with mild respirophasic inflow variations below tamponade criteria (mitral inflows 120.8 cm/s inspiration, 102 cm/s expiration; tricuspid inflows 75.2 cm/s inspiration, 104.8 cm/s expiration) and no chamber collapse. There was mild left ventricular hypertrophy and dilation with severely reduced ejection fraction of 20%–25%, right ventricular dilation, and a dilated non-collapsible inferior vena cava consistent with elevated right atrial pressure.

Contrast-enhanced CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis again showed a large pericardial effusion, extensive bulky ill-defined retroperitoneal soft tissue encasing both kidneys and adrenal glands with patchy renal hyperenhancement ('hairy kidney' appearance), and mild infrarenal abdominal aortic wall thickening ('coated aorta'), reported as concerning for an infiltrative process. Sclerotic and lytic osseous lesions involved the right clavicle, bilateral scapulae, left iliac wing, right posterior acetabulum and partially visualised left femur, with diffuse body wall anasarca, multiple right basilar pulmonary nodules up to 1.5 cm and mild hydronephrosis from the retroperitoneal mass.

Additional laboratory tests after imaging: B-type natriuretic peptide elevated at 951 pg/mL (normal <100 pg/mL), C-reactive protein 121.8 mg/L (normal <5 mg/L), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 77 mm/hour (normal <20 mm/hour). Lactate dehydrogenase, uric acid, human chorionic gonadotropin and alpha-fetoprotein were within normal limits. Serum and urine protein electrophoresis, urine free light chain, immunoelectrophoresis and serum immunoglobulins were within normal range. Peripheral blood flow cytometry showed no monotypic B-cell or immunophenotypically aberrant T-cell population.

Cardiac MRI with and without contrast showed a large simple pericardial effusion with no pericardial enhancement or tamponade, positive non-ischaemic late gadolinium enhancement at the mid inferior RV insertion site in a subendocardial pattern reported as non-specific, elevated postcontrast myocardial extracellular volume of 54.1% (normal 25%–30%), normal T2, biventricular dilatation with moderately impaired biventricular function (LV EF 40%, RV EF 28%). The study was limited by motion artefact from the pericardial and pleural effusions.

Recorded working considerations at this stage, documented as provisional: the initial presentation was apparently concerning for primary pericarditis or myopericarditis; ischaemic heart disease was also considered because of severe obesity and family history, though troponins were normal, the ECG showed no ischaemic or pericarditic changes, T2 was normal and the technically limited CMR showed only a non-specific RV insertion-site LGE focus, so active myopericarditis was not established. Echocardiography showed global rather than regional hypokinesis, CMR showed no ischaemic LGE pattern, the non-ECG-gated CT did not report coronary calcification, and occult coronary disease was not anatomically excluded. Tuberculosis was recorded as a possible differential, without identified risk factors, exposure or typical symptoms. The 'hairy kidney' appearance was recorded as narrowing differentials including LCH, Rosai-Dorfman disease, lymphoma, IgG4-related disease or other malignancy-related metastatic lesions.

Availability limits: this is a constructed selected-record review. No retroperitoneal biopsy, pericardial fluid sampling or pericardial biopsy has been performed at this assessment point, and no tissue, immunohistochemistry or molecular results are available. Pericardial fluid was not analysed. HbA1c and lipid profile were not obtained. Coronary anatomy was not assessed. No data are available on the patient's course beyond the imaging described; unreported information is unknown, not normal. Any proposed further tests below are candidates for planning only, not documented decisions.

prepared_template.title: Persistent shock after resuscitated ventricular fibrillation
prepared_template.facts:
A woman in her late 30s presented after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Before collapsing she had an episode of sudden-onset mild chest pain. A bystander started hands-only CPR and called 911. Emergency responders found her in ventricular fibrillation arrest; EMS initiated CPR with a mechanical device and she was defibrillated six times. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved by EMS before arrival in the emergency room.

She had no prior cardiac history. She had a remote history of opiate-use disorder, having last used heroin several years ago, and had bipolar 1, anxiety, depression and a history of mild cervical dysplasia. Admission medications included lexapro, clonazepam, clonidine, hydroxyzine, trazodone, venlafaxine and methadone.

Collateral history noted nausea, subjective fevers and a feeling that her skin was burning for about 3 days before presentation, with multiple episodes of vomiting. It was also noted that she tends to take her psychiatric medications all at once rather than spacing them through the day as prescribed.

In the emergency room she was tachycardic and hypotensive with mottled extremities. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus tachycardia at 115 bpm with diffuse T-wave inversions but no ST elevations. The QTc was prolonged to 605 ms.

Initial laboratory results included potassium 2.8 mEq/L, phosphate 11 mmol/L, creatinine 1.2 mg/dL (above her baseline), leukocytosis of 23 000 cells/mm³, lactate 13 mg/dL, alanine aminotransferase 527 U/L and aspartate aminotransferase 695 U/L. Haemoglobin was initially 12.6 g/dL and downtrended to 11.5 g/dL.

Echocardiography showed multiple wall motion abnormalities and an estimated left ventricular ejection fraction of 25%, raising concern for myocardial infarction. No nitrates were given at any point in the course.

The team also considered that hypotension from trazodone and clonidine might have led to the initial syncope, while noting this would not adequately explain the sustained ventricular fibrillation arrest.

Constructed selected-record review: this packet assembles facts recorded at the initial emergency department assessment and the team's contemporaneous differential. Findings obtained later (catheterisation and fluoroscopic findings, invasive haemodynamic data, any decompression, subsequent coronary assessment and clinical course) are withheld and must not be assumed. Unreported information is unknown, not normal; no pretreatment time point beyond the stated history is available.

cases.title: Active renal disease and uncertain drug exposure at early pregnancy confirmation
cases.summary:
Background
A woman in her 20s has beta-thalassaemia and SLE diagnosed two years earlier after nephrotic features and thrombocytopenia. The original kidney biopsy showed class III lupus nephritis, activity index 3/24 and chronicity 0/12. Prednisolone was used for six months with azathioprine, then stopped. She reports poor adherence to azathioprine and substantial prior steroid-associated weight gain. No RAAS-blocking antiproteinuric treatment was started while she was trying to conceive.
cases.purpose: Pregnancy, recent drug exposure, active disease, tolerability and adherence constrain treatment simultaneously. A favourable later outcome cannot establish that one regimen is universally preferable.
cases.source_note: The apparent two-dose versus later single-dose wording is not resolved by inventing earlier infusion dates. The original biopsy is kept historical, and pregnancy counselling/cessation already done are not presented as actions the model must newly perform. Gravida/para wording in the paper is not used to infer a missing obstetric chronology.

prepared_template.facts:
Background
A woman in her 20s has beta-thalassaemia and SLE diagnosed two years earlier after nephrotic features and thrombocytopenia. The original kidney biopsy showed class III lupus nephritis, activity index 3/24 and chronicity 0/12. Prednisolone was used for six months with azathioprine, then stopped. She reports poor adherence to azathioprine and substantial prior steroid-associated weight gain. No RAAS-blocking antiproteinuric treatment was started while she was trying to conceive.

Current relapse
Approximately two years after diagnosis she has recurrent rash, persistent joint/bone pain and pitting oedema in the arms and legs. C3 is 0.56 g/L and C4 0.06 g/L; anti-dsDNA is 28.3 IU/mL. Urine protein:creatinine ratio has risen from 152 to 215 mg/mmol, with urine blood ++ and protein +++. ESR is 54 mm/hour, haemoglobin 98 g/L, white cells 5.36 × 10^9/L and platelets 215 × 10^9/L. Creatinine is 36 micromol/L and eGFR above 90 mL/min/1.73 m². No repeat biopsy is supplied.

Treatment and pregnancy timeline
Azathioprine was changed to mycophenolate mofetil because of active disease, with counselling about avoiding pregnancy. The escalation account also refers to 'two doses of rituximab', but gives no administration dates; the records available here do not establish how many infusions had actually been administered by pregnancy confirmation. Three days after the treatment change, an unplanned pregnancy is confirmed at about five weeks' gestation. Mycophenolate is stopped immediately. The patient is counselled about exposure-related uncertainty and elects to continue the pregnancy.

Current decision
The revised renal/pregnancy regimen has not been provided. Exact mycophenolate doses and exposure dates, rituximab administration records, current BP, detailed obstetric assessment and current complete medication list are not supplied. The original nephritis class is historical; a current renal histological class is not established by a new biopsy. Later renal response, fetal monitoring, delivery and neonatal outcomes are withheld.

prepared_template.title: New abdominal fluid after shunting for a brainstem tumour
prepared_template.facts:
A boy in early childhood presented with a 4-month history of intermittent headaches, morning emesis and ataxic gait. Cranial MRI showed an expansile, infiltrative mass centred in the pons (53×46×56 mm), extending into the midbrain and medulla, with T2 hyperintensity, mass effect and near-complete effacement of the fourth ventricle. A presumptive radiographic diagnosis of diffuse midline glioma was made; no brain biopsy was performed. Whole-spine MRI at presentation demonstrated no drop metastases.

Because of obstructive hydrocephalus, a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt was inserted, followed by focal radiotherapy (54 Gy in 30 fractions). At local progression, the patient underwent re-irradiation (24 Gy in 12 fractions) and salvage dordaviprone (ONC201).

Twelve months following shunt placement, the patient developed abdominal distension and ascites from a large abdominal pseudocyst, indicating distal shunt failure without proximal obstruction or infection. No shunt tap was performed before operative shunt externalisation and pseudocyst drainage.

At operative shunt externalisation and pseudocyst drainage, CSF drawn from the ventricular catheter was clear and colourless, with 2 nucleated cells/µL and 0 erythrocytes/µL. Cytology was reported negative for malignant cells. Only a 0.3 mL aliquot reached cytology, which was insufficient for a cell block and showed only blood, fibrin and macrophages.

This is a constructed selected-record review. The ventricular-catheter CSF findings were obtained at operative shunt externalisation and pseudocyst drainage. No shunt tap was performed before surgery. Subsequent peritoneal sampling, laparoscopy, biopsy, molecular testing and later clinical-course results are withheld.

The initial radiographic diagnosis of diffuse midline glioma remains presumptive in the record: it was made radiographically without brain biopsy, and no tissue diagnosis of the brainstem lesion exists at this decision point.

prepared_template.title: Recurrent dizziness with several partially supported explanations
prepared_template.facts:
A man in his 60s was referred to otolaryngology for recurrent vertigo and unsteadiness. Neurological examination was normal apart from a positive Romberg test; Dix-Hallpike testing revealed leftward horizontal nystagmus lasting approximately 20 seconds in the head-hanging position, interpreted as left posterior canal BPPV, with fatigue but no subjective vertigo. Central vertigo was excluded on clinical grounds.

A Schellong test demonstrated a significant postural blood-pressure drop, recorded as 122/76 supine, 104/62 immediately on standing and 100/60 mm Hg after 10 minutes standing, with pulse 80, 93 and 92 bpm, confirming orthostatic dysregulation. Caloric testing, VEMP testing and video head impulse test gains showed normal responses, indicating no significant canal paresis or vestibular hypofunction. Psychogenic dizziness was excluded on the basis of low anxiety and stress scores.

His regular medications included levomepromazine 25 mg (0.5 tablet/day), ethyl loflazepate 2 mg (1 tablet/day), suvorexant 20 mg (1 tablet/day) and clonazepam 1 mg (1 tablet/day). He reported occasional episodes of excessive alcohol consumption, including nearly a full bottle of 70% rum or an entire 1.8 L bottle of wine without somnolence. He had ceased heavy smoking approximately 4 months before presentation; intermittent alcohol use persisted.

Approximately 3 years before presentation he developed severe unsteadiness, which he attributed to sedative-hypnotic use, with episodes of rotatory vertigo lasting several minutes to nearly 1 hour while standing during the day. Approximately 4 months before presentation, about 30% of vertigo episodes occurred on awakening in the morning, either spontaneously or with head movement, and were more pronounced in severity. There were no auditory symptoms, headache or focal neurological deficits.

Comorbidities included 'other specified bipolar and related disorders with hypomanic episodes without prior depressive episodes', with mood instability, suspected developmental traits, insomnia from age 59 years, and compression fractures due to stumbling and falling at age 62 years. At the initial assessment the presentation was recorded as consistent with multifactorial vertigo, likely involving BPPV, orthostatic dysregulation, hypnotic-related disequilibrium and medication-induced dizziness; this remained a working formulation rather than a confirmed single cause. Despite being informed of potential drug-related effects, the patient chose to continue his medications.

One month after presentation, cardiology evaluation with echocardiography and carotid ultrasonography was unremarkable; orthostatic dysregulation and medication-induced dizziness were considered most likely. He was advised to taper hypnotics and rise gradually but declined changes. Ryokeijutsukanto was initiated by the ENT department, yielding partial symptomatic improvement.

Four months after presentation he had several minutes of rotatory vertigo on rising from bed; examination confirmed recurrent left posterior canal BPPV, and symptoms improved following an Epley manoeuvre. Eight months after presentation he fell from a 2 m loft and struck his left flank; flunitrazepam use may have contributed. He had also lost substantial weight, from 85 to 73 kg, despite normal liver function, and was advised to increase protein and calcium intake.

Nine months after presentation, laboratory data were notable only for glucose 192 mg/dL and HbA1c 5.9%. Hypertriglyceridaemia and hyperuricaemia were diagnosed and treated with febuxostat and pemafibrate at another hospital. No glucose measurement during any symptomatic episode is recorded up to this point.

Eleven months after presentation, he fell again without vertigo but subsequently experienced vague lightheadedness and visual distortion. He also reported intermittent non-vertiginous lightheadedness, particularly during fasting or standing, which the record suggests may reflect ongoing autonomic and metabolic contributions.

Fourteen months after presentation, he collapsed at 3 a.m. while fasting; imaging showed no injury. Because all prior vertigo episodes had occurred during fasting and his casual glucose level had been elevated, fasting-related hypoglycaemia associated with glucose intolerance was suspected, and further evaluation with CGM was recommended by the otolaryngologist. This suspicion is documented as a hypothesis; no confirmatory glucose measurement during an episode is recorded at this decision point.

This is a constructed selected-record review: the findings above were documented at different times over fourteen months, and no single pre-treatment time point contains all of them. The record does not state whether any glucose, postural or medication data were captured during the episodes themselves, and unreported measurements should be treated as unknown rather than normal. The CGM recommendation at fourteen months is a proposed future investigation, not a documented result.

Candidate essential information requirements (unconfirmed candidates, justified by the presentation of recurrent early-morning collapse with coexisting vestibular, postural and sedative findings): (1) Episode-linked glucose measurement during symptoms, obtainable by continuous glucose monitoring or, as a clinically equivalent alternative, timed finger-prick capillary glucose during typical early-morning windows and at symptom onset, over the coming days to weeks; this would distinguish hypoglycaemia from coexisting causes. (2) Episode-linked posture, medication-timing and alcohol information around each event, obtainable from a symptom diary with lying/standing blood pressure readings and a documented medication and alcohol timeline, obtainable within days; this would separate orthostatic and sedative or alcohol effects from metabolic causes. Both are proposed requests, not documented decisions.

prepared_template.title: Severe apathy despite biochemical improvement in thyroid function
prepared_template.facts:
Constructed selected-record review: the facts below were documented at different times and are presented together for assessment at the chosen decision point (after thyroid treatment, empirical corticosteroids and brain imaging, but before any CSF drainage procedure). No single pretreatment time point is implied, and later responses are not available at this point.

Patient and course: A woman in her 60s with no relevant medical history developed progressive apathy over a 2-year period, having previously lived independently and remained employed until symptom onset. She eventually became largely bedbound with markedly reduced oral intake requiring enteral feeding.

Examination findings at presentation: severe apathy, general fatigue and constipation. Urinary incontinence was absent. No frontal release signs (grasp, snout), no rigidity, tremor or clinical parkinsonism; eye movements and other reflexes were normal. Profound loss of initiation prevented reliable formal gait assessment. The admission modified Rankin Scale score was 5. There was no history of seizures, impaired consciousness or a fluctuating encephalopathic course.

Thyroid tests and treatment: initial TSH 10.8 mIU/L, free T4 11.2 pmol/L (0.87 ng/dL), thyroid peroxidase antibodies 442 IU/mL and thyroglobulin antibodies 691 IU/mL. Levothyroxine was started at 25 μg/day. Two months later TSH had fallen to 5.4 mIU/L and free T4 risen to 21.8 pmol/L (1.69 ng/dL), but the neurological symptoms were unchanged.

Recorded working diagnoses at this stage: hypothyroidism was initially considered because of fatigue, constipation and the thyroid results; persistent severe impairment despite biochemical improvement prompted investigation of an additional neurological cause. Persistent severe neuropsychiatric symptoms with positive thyroid autoantibodies also prompted consideration of possible thyroid-associated autoimmune encephalopathy, and an empirical course of methylprednisolone (1000 mg/day for 3 days) produced no clear improvement in apathy or functional status. Anti-NAE antibody testing was negative, with results available after the corticosteroid course. These remain provisional, documented hypotheses, not confirmed diagnoses.

Imaging: brain CT showed progressive ventriculomegaly compared with imaging 4 years earlier; the Evans index increased from 0.252 to 0.325 and the callosal angle decreased from 104.6° to 67.6°, with a disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus (DESH) pattern. Brain MRI confirmed ventriculomegaly with no abnormal DWI hyperintensity or other significant findings beyond the hydrocephalic changes. The clinical history and imaging revealed no antecedent cause of secondary hydrocephalus.

Cognition and behavioural ratings available at this point: the MMSE score before the tap test was 5/30. Retrospectively reconstructed family ratings of the preoperative state (obtained later and therefore susceptible to recall bias) gave an NPI apathy/indifference domain score of 12 (frequency 4 × severity 3), an NPI depression/dysphoria domain score of 0, and an AES-I-J total score of 57 (range 18–72, higher indicating greater apathy).

Documented differential considerations recorded around this assessment, without a confirmed cause: an autoimmune encephalitic process was considered less likely given the slowly progressive 2-year course without seizures or fluctuating consciousness, unremarkable routine CSF findings and absence of additional MRI abnormalities; the negative anti-NAE result was not used to exclude Hashimoto encephalopathy/SREAT given the limited diagnostic utility of the antibody, and thyroid autoantibody positivity alone does not establish central nervous system autoimmunity. Depression was considered; the predominant behavioural feature was marked reduction in spontaneous goal-directed activity. Neurodegenerative and other frontal-subcortical disorders were also in the differential.

Availability limits at this decision point: gait could not be assessed because of severe apathy — this is an unassessable feature, not a documented absence of gait disturbance. Urinary incontinence was documented as absent. No CSF drainage procedure, drainage response, shunt surgery or post-treatment outcome is available at this point; such data, if any exist, are withheld. Unreported items are unknown, not normal.

prepared_template.title: Recurrent impaired consciousness with documented hypoglycaemia
prepared_template.facts:
An adolescent boy presented to the paediatric outpatient department with multiple transient episodes of loss of consciousness over the preceding 4 years. Both the frequency and the duration of these episodes increased progressively over this period. Their frequency rose from 1 to 2 per week to 3–4 per day, and the duration of each episode lengthened from 1 to 2 min to 2–3 min. Episodes were preceded by lethargy, nausea and sweating, were characterised by altered sensorium and unresponsiveness, and resolved after administration of glucose with restoration of consciousness, rather than remitting spontaneously. The family did not routinely seek medical attention for individual episodes until symptoms began to worsen in the month before presentation. At that time, he also developed headache of acute onset, mild-to-moderate intensity, intermittent and frontal in location, accompanied by forgetfulness, confusion and vomiting twice a day.

He came from a resource-limited rural community. His mother was in apparent good health. His father had been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus 7 years earlier and was managed with lifestyle modification and diet alone. He had one sibling, a sister, with no significant medical history.

On detailed history, the family described recurrent episodes of faintness, myalgia, paraesthesia and unexplained irritability, along with unusual hunger and tachycardia occurring predominantly in the morning or after physical exertion. The myalgia was attributed to generalised muscular exertion during convulsive, seizure-like motor activity accompanying the more severe episodes. Electroencephalography was not performed, and a primary epileptic disorder was therefore not formally excluded.

Four years earlier, at the onset of these symptoms, he had been admitted to another tertiary care institute, where capillary/plasma glucose during symptomatic episodes ranged from 20 to 38 mg/dL and normalised promptly with intravenous glucose. The referral summary available to us records that a circulating insulin level was measured at that admission and reported as normal. However, the numerical value, the assay used, and whether the sample was drawn concurrently with a documented low glucose cannot be established, as the primary records from that institution are not retrievable. No other biochemical marker of hyperinsulinism (C-peptide, free fatty acids, beta-hydroxybutyrate or the glycaemic response to glucagon) was assessed at that admission. Abdominal ultrasonography and contrast-enhanced abdominal CT were also reported as normal, and he was discharged with a diagnosis of 'idiopathic intermittent hypoglycaemia'.

On the current presentation, he appeared lethargic and unwell but was easily arousable, oriented and haemodynamically stable, with normal skin colour. His height was 168 cm (SD score −0.39), weight 68.4 kg (SD score +0.72) and body mass index 24.2 kg/m² (SD score +0.96). By the revised Indian Academy of Pediatrics 2015 growth charts, which define overweight in 5–18 year-olds by the adult-equivalent body mass index cut-off of 23 rather than by an SD-score threshold, he was overweight at presentation. Vital signs were as follows: temperature 36.9 C (98.4°F), heart rate 100 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min and blood pressure 100/67 mm Hg without orthostatic change. Systemic examination was otherwise unremarkable. The peripheries were cool. The abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds and no palpable mass.

During observation he again became symptomatic with headache. Capillary glucose at that time was 48 mg/dL, and his symptoms resolved promptly after intravenous dextrose. A bolus of 25% dextrose was administered for this acute symptomatic episode, with capillary glucose rising to 79 mg/dL and resolution of symptoms within 15 min. He was subsequently maintained on intravenous 10% dextrose saline infusion with 2 hourly glucose monitoring.

Record limits: this is a constructed selected-record review. The earlier insulin result exists only as a referral summary stating 'normal'; its numerical value, assay and timing relative to a documented low glucose cannot be recovered because the primary records of the earlier institution are not retrievable. The earlier imaging reports are likewise available only as reported summaries, and the original images were not retrievable for direct comparison. No paired critical sample, C-peptide, ketone, free fatty acid, counter-regulatory hormone or sulfonylurea measurements are documented at the current decision point. Unreported data are unknown, not normal.

The documented discharge label from the earlier admission was 'idiopathic intermittent hypoglycaemia'; this is recorded as a prior working diagnosis, not a confirmed explanation. Electroencephalography was not performed, so a primary epileptic disorder was not formally excluded. A sulfonylurea screen was not performed at the earlier admission, and no household access to sulfonylurea agents is recorded in the available history.

prepared_template.title: New neurological decline after prolonged control of a spinal tumour
prepared_template.facts:
Constructed selected-record review: the facts below were documented at different times (months 0 to 41) and are assembled retrospectively from the records of two institutions; no single pretreatment or admission-day time point contains all of them. The assessment point is month 41, at readmission, before restaging MRI.

The patient is a retired woman in her mid-70s, previously independent, with levothyroxine-treated hypothyroidism. She initially presented with a 4-month history of progressive bilateral hand dysesthesia and left-predominant quadriparesis; examination showed myelopathic signs, ASIA impairment scale C at the C4 neurological level, and ECOG performance status 3.

Initial cervical MRI (1 week before surgery) showed a left-sided dumbbell-shaped intradural lesion spanning C3–C6 with a cord-compressing component and an extraspinal component extending through the left C4–C5 neural foramen; it enhanced after gadolinium. Imaging was non-specific and the radiological impression was meningioma.

Histopathology of the resected tumour showed a densely cellular melanocytic neoplasm with brown intracellular pigment, strongly positive for Melan-A, HMB-45 and S-100, negative for cytokeratin; BRAF testing was wild-type. Ki-67, GNAQ/GNA11 hot-spot sequencing, PD-L1 expression and CD8-positive tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte density were not assessed. Cerebrospinal fluid was not examined at diagnosis or at progression.

Staging followed Hayward criteria: whole-body 18F-FDG PET-CT at week 2 showed uptake confined to the cervical lesion; brain MRI at week 3 was normal; complete dermatological examination found no suspicious lesion and funduscopy excluded an ocular primary. Punch biopsies of two pigmented skin lesions at month 13 were benign. The diagnosis of primary intramedullary spinal cord melanoma (PISCM) was established.

At month 0 she underwent posterior cervical laminectomy with microsurgical resection. The extraspinal component was removed entirely with preservation of the nerve root; the intramedullary component was subtotally resected, leaving a layer of approximately 1 mm where no cleavage plane could be found between tumour and functional cord. Adjuvant radiotherapy, 20 Gy in five fractions to C2–C6, was delivered in week 6; pembrolizumab 2 mg/kg every 28 days was started in week 5, 3 days before radiotherapy began, so there is no pre-ICI imaging interval.

Neurological recovery was progressive: by month 5 she had full hand function and walked 30 m with a walker; by month 18 she stood unaided and walked short distances without aids; from month 27 to 36 she walked with a walker used for balance, and ECOG improved from 3 to 2. At month 27, a multidisciplinary review judged the stable enhancing tissue at the operative site compatible with tumour stabilised under treatment, and pembrolizumab was continued. Therapy was held at month 29 for acute cholecystitis and community-acquired pneumonia, resumed at month 33, and continued thereafter.

Surveillance PET-CT at months 4, 9, 13, 25 and 31 showed no metabolically active disease. Cervical MRI at months 7, 18, 27 and 36 showed stable enhancing tissue at the operative site, read by the treating surgeon as probable scar. The report notes that the stable enhancing residual was never distinguishable from scar on imaging alone, and that CSF was not sampled in the supplied surveillance record.

At month 41, routine PET-CT showed mildly increased uptake in the C3–C6 operative bed. Within days she developed progressive left-sided weakness and was readmitted. No restaging MRI at this admission is documented in the material available at this decision point; the results of any further imaging, histology, treatment decisions and outcome after readmission are not supplied and must be treated as unknown.

Documented interpretation limits relevant to this point: no formal response criteria were applied prospectively; disease status was followed by PET-CT and contrast MRI against a pre-treatment baseline. The month 27 multidisciplinary decision to continue pembrolizumab rested on reasoning that apparent progression within 6 months of starting immunotherapy should be confirmed on repeat imaging unless the patient is clinically worse. Radiotherapy and pembrolizumab started in the same week, so neither the period of control nor any relapse can be attributed to either modality.

prepared_template.title: Proteinuric renal disease with inconsistent autoimmune and clonal clues
prepared_template.facts:
A woman in her 70s was referred for urgent outpatient review from respiratory clinic with dyspnoea and oedema. Her background included cystic lung disease without a known genetic variant, hypertension, vascular disease with previous coeliac artery stenosis and left vertebral artery dissection, obstructive sleep apnoea, and eclampsia with her second child.

On examination she was hypertensive, up to 207/81 mmHg, saturating 100% on room air, with a clear chest but raised jugular venous pressure and severe peripheral oedema to the level of the inguinal ligament.

Initial biochemistry: creatinine 158 µmol/L, urea 23 mmol/L, albumin 30 g/L. Urine albumin–creatinine ratio 232.3 mg/mmol, protein–creatinine ratio 332 mg/mmol, and 64×10^6/L dysmorphic erythrocytes on microscopy and culture. Coagulation showed no coagulopathy with an INR <0.9.

Autoimmune serology at initial assessment: ANA titre 1:640 with a homogenous pattern, but anti-dsDNA 3 IU/mL (normal <7 IU/mL). Myeloperoxidase-ANCA, proteinase 3-ANCA and anti-GBM antibodies were all negative. C3 was 1.20 g/L and C4 0.30 g/L, both within the normal range.

Infection and clonal screening at initial assessment: hepatitis C, HIV, hepatitis B surface antigens and core antibodies were negative. ASOT and Quantiferon gold were negative. Cryoglobulins were not detected. Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrated a small IgG (kappa) band of trace amount on a background of an oligoclonal pattern; serum kappa/lambda ratio was 1.54 and urine Bence-Jones proteins were negative.

Complement dysregulation testing recorded around this evaluation: C3 nephritic factor was negative and genetic testing was negative for identified mutations in the CFHR3/1 and CFB genes. The source reports these alongside the initial investigations; the exact sampling dates relative to the biopsy are not separately stated, so this is a constructed selected-record review.

Imaging: ultrasound of the renal tract confirmed normal appearances of both kidneys. CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis did not demonstrate any occult infection, malignancy or thymoma.

Renal biopsy (22 glomeruli, 1 globally sclerosed): diffuse glomerular enlargement with increased mesangial and endocapillary cellularity and accentuated tuft lobularity. Silver staining showed increased mesangial matrix, glomerular basement membrane double contouring and mesangial cell interposition. Mesangial and intramembranous fuscinophilic deposits were present. There were no glomerular necrotising lesions or crescents; one artery showed mild intimal thickening but no vasculitis; no interstitial fibrosis or tubular atrophy.

Immunohistochemistry: strong positive staining for C3 and C1q in the glomerular mesangial capillary loop; moderate staining for IgG in the mesangial capillary loop, IgM in the glomerular capillary loop and C4 in the glomerular mesangial capillary loop; weaker IgA staining in mesangial and glomerular capillary loops. Electron microscopy showed small and large electron-dense deposits of small fibrils in the mesangial matrix and along the subendothelial aspect of the glomerular basement membrane; there was no dense deposit disease. Immunoperoxidase staining for DNAJB9, amyloid A and Congo red were all negative.

The deposit fibrils had an average measured width of 7.3 nm on high-power electron microscopy.

Availability limits: this packet deliberately withholds later repeat protein studies, any subsequent neuromuscular findings, antibody results, electromyography, treatment responses and outcome. Data reported in the source at different time points (for example complement and genetic testing reported alongside three-month serial results) are presented here only as far as they are documented; no pretreatment time point beyond the recorded initial assessment is claimed, and unreported information is unknown rather than normal.

prepared_template.title: Mixed prostate histology despite widespread tracer-avid disease
prepared_template.facts:
Constructed selected-record review. This packet assembles case data recorded at different times (imaging 21 May 2025 to 3 July 2025; biopsies reported thereafter) around a treatment-planning decision point. It is a retrospective written record, not a live encounter; no pretreatment time point beyond the documented dates is claimed.

A man in his late 70s presented with progressively worsening lower back pain, generalised weakness and decreased mobility for 3 months, with anorexia and weight loss. He reported no haematuria, dysuria or bowel disturbances. There was no prior history of prostate malignancy or hormonal therapy.

On examination he was pale with stable vitals. Digital rectal examination revealed an enlarged, irregular, firm prostate. Systemic examination was otherwise unremarkable except for diffuse spinal tenderness.

Laboratory investigations showed serum PSA of 247 ng/mL, mild anaemia (haemoglobin 10.2 g/dL) and elevated alkaline phosphatase. No other laboratory values, performance status, comorbidity or organ-function data are reported in the supplied record.

MRI lumbosacral spine (21 May 2025) showed multiple patchy marrow signal abnormalities throughout cervical, dorsal and lumbar vertebrae and bilateral pelvic bones, involving posterior elements, with a lobulated retroperitoneal soft-tissue mass along bilateral iliac vessels suggesting extensive lymphadenopathy. No cord compression was noted.

Contrast-enhanced CT chest, abdomen and pelvis (24 May 2025) showed an enlarged prostate (5.5×4.8 cm) with heterogeneous enhancement, extensive retroperitoneal and bilateral iliac lymphadenopathy (largest short-axis diameter 36 mm), mixed lytic–sclerotic skeletal lesions involving sacrum, iliac bones, vertebrae and ribs, mild bilateral pleural effusions, bibasal atelectasis and pathological fractures of the right clavicle and ribs 7–8.

PSMA PET–CT (3 July 2025) demonstrated a diffusely PSMA-avid prostate (SUV_max 10.7), multistation tracer-avid lymphadenopathy (paraaortic SUV 10.7; external iliac SUV 9.8; inguinal SUV 11.9) and widespread skeletal metastases including clivus (SUV 32.9), sternum (SUV 35.9), D12 vertebra (SUV 20.7) and sacrum (SUV 17.5). No PSMA-avid visceral lesions were detected.

prepared_template.title: An apparent duodenal mass with progressive anaemia after surgery
prepared_template.facts:
A woman in her early twenties presented with persistent mild right upper quadrant pain, progressive fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance. She had undergone an uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic cholelithiasis 2 months before presentation, with uneventful immediate postoperative recovery.

One month after surgery she developed mild, dull-aching, non-radiating right hypochondrial pain that was gradually progressive, with increasing fatigue over the following weeks. She denied haematemesis, melaena, haematochezia, jaundice, fever, vomiting, chest pain, cough, weight loss and anorexia. There was no history of previous anaemia, jaundice, blood transfusion, iron supplementation, anticoagulant use or known bleeding disorder.

On examination she was haemodynamically stable with pallor; icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy and peripheral oedema were absent. Abdominal examination showed mild right hypochondrial tenderness without guarding or rigidity, and mild splenomegaly was noted. Digital rectal examination showed normal-coloured stool with no evidence of melaena or fresh blood.

Initial laboratory investigations showed normocytic normochromic anaemia with haemoglobin 8.7 g/dL, declining to 7.6 g/dL over the subsequent week. Total leucocyte count was 5240 cells/mm³ and platelet count 2.41 lakh cells/mm³. Liver biochemistry: total bilirubin 0.87 mg/dL (direct 0.47 mg/dL), AST 10.18 IU/L, ALT 22.42 IU/L, alkaline phosphatase 104 IU/L. Total protein 5.39 g/dL, albumin 3.09 g/dL. Prothrombin time 15.10, INR 1.13, blood urea 14.70 mg/dL, creatinine 0.47 mg/dL. Amylase 23.21 IU/L and lipase 36.34 IU/L.

Iron studies showed low serum iron (39 µg/dL) and transferrin saturation (16%), low total iron-binding capacity (235 µg/dL) and markedly elevated serum ferritin (724 ng/mL), a pattern the report described as suggestive of iron-restricted erythropoiesis in the setting of inflammation. Faecal occult blood testing was positive. Vitamin B12 was 376 ng/L (206–678 ng/L) and folic acid 11.30 ng/L (3.1–20.5 ng/L).

Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy demonstrated a 2×2 cm soft, erythematous, sessile nodular lesion arising from the inferior wall of the first part of the duodenum, with smooth well-defined margins, intact overlying mucosa and no ulceration. There was no evidence of active bleeding or haemobilia at the time of endoscopy.

Documented decision at endoscopy: given the unusual appearance in a patient with a recent laparoscopic cholecystectomy, biopsy was deferred because of concern for an underlying vascular lesion. This is recorded as a clinical concern at the time, not a confirmed diagnosis.

Recorded working considerations at this stage: the endoscopic appearance of a duodenal mass with progressive anaemia prompted consideration of both vascular and neoplastic lesions, including gastrointestinal stromal tumour or Brunner gland hamartoma; the recent laparoscopic cholecystectomy prompted consideration of a postoperative vascular complication first. Apart from hepatic artery pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous malformation and cystic artery pseudoaneurysm were also considered. These are documented as differential considerations only; no confirmatory imaging had been performed at this decision point.

Availability limits and record construction: this is a constructed selected-record review. The endoscopy preceded CT angiography in this case because of progressive anaemia, suspected occult gastrointestinal blood loss and delayed radiology availability; the report states this sequence was specific to the circumstances of this case. No vascular imaging (Doppler ultrasonography, CT angiography or digital subtraction angiography) results are available at this decision point. Whether a direct communication between any lesion and the duodenal lumen exists has not been demonstrated, and the mechanism of occult blood loss remains uncertain. Unreported information is unknown, not normal.

prepared_template.title: Prolonged asystolic episodes in a very young patient
prepared_template.facts:
A patient in her late teens presented to the emergency department with syncope accompanied by a 'seizure-like' episode. At home she stood up to stretch, felt dizzy and collapsed; her mother found her rigid and shaking, with eyes rolled back and cyanotic lips. Ambulance paramedics documented her as drowsy, reporting dull chest pain and palpitations. Her initial ECG showed sinus tachycardia (ventricular rate 100 bpm), first-degree AV block with a PR interval of 220 ms, and a corrected QT interval of 400 ms.

She reported similar episodes over the past 5 years, typically triggered by emotional distress (for example during a blood test) and following physical injury. In the 6 months prior to this presentation the episodes had become more frequent and severe. Her medical history included anxiety with autism spectrum and sleep disorder, for which she took regular mirtazapine. There was no significant family history of syncope, epilepsy, arrhythmias or sudden cardiac death.

En route to hospital she became markedly pale with a reduced Glasgow Coma Scale score of 12/15. Sequential ECG monitoring captured rapid progression from Mobitz type II second-degree AV block to complete heart block with a narrow QRS escape rhythm (40 bpm), culminating in ventricular standstill lasting over 20 s with apnoea. High flow oxygen and transcutaneous pacing were administered by the ambulance team, with return of spontaneous ventricular activity, pulse and blood pressure. She then maintained sinus rhythm with stable vital signs: pulse 45 beats per minute (sinus bradycardia), blood pressure 109/64 mm Hg, temperature 36.3°C, respiratory rate 20/min and SpO2 99% on room air. Physical examination, including cardiac auscultation, was unremarkable.

An extensive panel of blood tests (complete blood count, urea and electrolytes, thyroid function test, high sensitivity troponin, serum lactate and liver function test) was within normal limits. Chest radiograph showed clear lung fields and normal mediastinal contours. A formal transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated normal biventricular size and systolic function, with no valvular abnormalities or abnormal shunts. She was placed on in-patient cardiac monitoring in a coronary care unit.

During 7-day in-patient cardiac monitoring she was actively symptomatic with dizzy episodes, with correlating intermittent 2:1 AV block and P-wave asystole lasting up to 9 s.

In the absence of any rate limiting medications that would have contributed to the profound bradycardia and asystole, and based on her clear history and documented ECG changes, a working diagnosis of profound cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope was made. Differential diagnoses included situational syncope and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome; these were thought unlikely on the basis of multiple episodes of AV dissociation and bradycardia occurring even in the absence of any triggers. An urgent electrophysiology opinion was obtained to guide management.

Initial management focused on conservative measures and pharmacological intervention with midodrine. These failed to mitigate her symptoms and the risk of loss of consciousness associated with these prolonged episodes. The patient, prioritising symptom resolution, requested definitive therapy.

Relevant guideline context recorded in the source: expert consensus statements and pacing guidelines endorse permanent pacing only for adults aged 40 years or older for cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope with documented asystolic pauses and refractory symptoms, creating a therapeutic challenge for clinicians managing younger patients with high-risk presentations and forcing reliance on individualised decision-making outside established guidelines.

The source also records that the diagnosis in this case was established through history and continuous cardiac monitoring during hospitalisation, without resort to a formal tilt table test, and that the tilt table test is otherwise described as the primary diagnostic tool for confirming cardioinhibitory vasovagal syncope. No tilt table test result is reported in the available record.

Constructed selected-record review: the available record combines data acquired at different times (pre-hospital monitoring, initial emergency department assessment, inpatient investigations over a 7-day admission, and guideline context from the article's background and discussion). The decision point under assessment is after the documented recurrent monitored events and after initial conservative measures and midodrine failed to control events, and before any permanent pacemaker selection. Device choice, counselling details, consent outcome, implantation and subsequent course are not part of the visible record for this assessment.

Unreported information in the visible record includes: any formal tilt table test; detailed documentation of the specific conservative measures trialled and their duration; a formal electrophysiology study; ambulatory (Holter or implantable loop recorder) monitoring before or after admission; and any documented discussion content of the multidisciplinary consultation. These are unknown, not established as normal or as not performed.
