prepared_template.title: Unequal bilateral ocular deterioration after systemic febrile illness
prepared_template.facts:
A man in his early 60s presented to eye casualty with acute right-sided vision loss and decreased visual acuity in the left eye. He had returned from Malaysia five days earlier; during the trip he underwent dental cleaning and four restorative dental fillings.

Three days after the dental treatment he developed fever, rigours, drowsiness and myalgia. By the time he returned to the United Kingdom the systemic symptoms had partially improved, but intermittent episodes of confusion had been noted.

His medical history included supraventricular tachycardia and psoriasis. There was no established history of diabetes mellitus, no evidence of prior immunosuppression, and no history of recent ocular surgery or trauma.

On ocular examination, visual acuity was counting fingers in the right eye and 6/9 in the left eye. The right eye showed 2+ anterior chamber cells, 2+ vitreous cells, retinitis above the superior vascular arcade, and retinal haemorrhages with pale centres consistent with Roth spots. A focal area of retinitis was present in the left eye.

The presence of bilateral ocular inflammation alongside a recent systemic febrile illness prompted investigation for an endogenous infective cause. This was a working suspicion at the time; the infective focus had not yet been identified while blood cultures were pending.

He was admitted under the medical team, where blood cultures and systemic investigations were requested. Initial systemic investigations demonstrated a significant inflammatory response and deranged liver biochemistry. Blood cultures initially reported Gram-negative bacilli, prompting treatment for Gram-negative septicaemia and further investigation, including imaging, to determine the underlying infective focus.

The documented initial differential reasoning noted that, with no history of ocular trauma or intraocular surgery, exogenous endophthalmitis was ruled out and an infective cause was deemed more likely. Given the bilateral nature and rapid progression, a non-infective aetiology including bilateral panuveitis secondary to an underlying systemic inflammatory or autoimmune condition was considered, and vasculitis and uveitis screening was requested. Masquerade syndromes such as lymphoma were also considered.

Documented management at this stage: he was treated with intravenous meropenem while awaiting microbiology details and further investigation for the primary source. Initial ocular treatment included topical levofloxacin to the right eye, topical corticosteroid therapy to both eyes and cycloplegia.

Availability limits at this assessment point: the blood-culture organism has not yet been identified beyond Gram-negative bacilli; no source imaging results are available; no intraocular microbiological samples have been reported. Later imaging, organism identification, ocular molecular results, surgical decisions and outcomes are not supplied and must not be assumed. Unreported information is unknown, not normal.

prepared_template.title: Recurrent transient deficits with an incompletely characterised intracranial stenosis
prepared_template.facts:
A man in his early 30s, previously independent and functionally well, presented to the emergency department with recurrent episodes of transient left-sided weakness and paraesthesia, each resolving spontaneously within approximately 10 minutes. Because of the recurrent stereotyped nature of the events, he was admitted to the stroke unit with a working diagnosis of crescendo transient ischaemic attacks. This working diagnosis remains provisional at the assessment point.

His only identified conventional vascular risk factor was hyperlipidaemia. He reported no recent systemic illness and no recent head or neck trauma. He was an ex-smoker, having stopped 3 months before presentation, with an estimated 10 pack-year history. He did not consume alcohol and denied recreational drug use. Detailed family history identified no stroke, cerebrovascular disease, arterial dissection, aneurysmal disease or known hereditary connective tissue disorder among first-degree relatives, and no personal history of childhood central nervous system infection or cranial radiotherapy. He reported chickenpox in childhood but no recent zoster rash or herpetic lesions. Neurological and systemic examination was unremarkable, with no phenotypic features suggestive of an inherited connective tissue disorder. In the absence of a suggestive phenotype or relevant family history, targeted genetic testing was not pursued.

Non-contrast CT of the brain on presentation was unremarkable. CT angiography of the head and neck performed the following day demonstrated narrowing of the distal M1 segment of the right middle cerebral artery. On this basis he was started on dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin 75 mg once a day and clopidogrel 75 mg once a day, alongside high-intensity statin therapy, in keeping with management of a high-risk transient ischaemic attack/minor ischaemic stroke presentation.

MRI of the brain with contrast and magnetic resonance angiography, performed 9 days after admission, demonstrated faint diffusion-weighted imaging hyperintensity with corresponding faint apparent diffusion coefficient hypointensity in the right putaminal region, consistent with restricted diffusion. Gadolinium-enhanced sequences demonstrated an enhancing lesion in the right basal ganglia, favoured to represent a subacute infarct. Magnetic resonance angiography demonstrated signal abnormality in the right M1 segment; however, the underlying vessel wall pathology remained difficult to characterise on standard sequences, and the appearances could not reliably distinguish severe stenosis from early occlusion or identify the underlying aetiology.

A comprehensive investigation panel was performed during the inpatient admission and is summarised in the article's table 1 (the table contents are not reproduced in this record). An electroencephalogram was performed 10 days after presentation because of the recurrent stereotyped nature of the episodes; this was unremarkable, making an epileptic mimic less likely in the clinical context.

The case was discussed at a neuroradiology multidisciplinary meeting. Given the atypical imaging appearances and persistent diagnostic uncertainty, including the uncharacterised right M1 abnormality and enhancing basal ganglia lesion, referral to a tertiary neurovascular centre for vessel wall imaging was recommended. The differential considered at that meeting included central nervous system vasculitis, moyamoya disease and other intracranial vasculopathies, and vessel wall imaging was requested specifically to help distinguish between them. The right basal ganglia lesion was felt to be more consistent with subacute infarction than demyelination, and cerebrospinal fluid assessment was reassuring apart from a borderline isolated protein elevation.

The principal diagnostic considerations recorded at this stage were central nervous system vasculitis, neuroinflammatory disease, intracranial atherosclerosis, moyamoya disease, seizure mimic and focal intracranial arterial dissection. These are documented differential considerations, not established diagnoses.

prepared_template.title: Highly suspicious breast imaging with an indeterminate core biopsy
prepared_template.facts:
A woman in her late 70s with hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia and hypothyroidism presented with a 6-week history of a painless left breast lump. She was a non-smoker with no personal or family history of breast or ovarian cancer, and no skin changes, nipple discharge or systemic symptoms. A 3-cm mass was palpated at the 6 o'clock position of the left breast, classified P5 (highly suspicious for malignancy), with no skin tethering, nipple inversion or palpable axillary lymphadenopathy.

Mammography showed a heterogeneous left breast mass measuring 20 mm x 27 mm x 27 mm, predominantly well-circumscribed but with focal areas of reduced border definition, classified M5 (highly suspicious of malignancy). The contralateral breast was reported normal.

Ultrasound of the left breast showed a solitary heterogeneous lesion measuring 29 mm x 19 mm x 24 mm with marked posterior acoustic shadowing, classified U5. No axillary lymphadenopathy was identified.

Core biopsy revealed a heterogeneous epithelial proliferation with lobulated nests of epithelial cells showing squamous differentiation. No definitive breast acini were identified. Immunohistochemistry on core biopsy showed patchy p63 positivity, and smooth muscle myosin highlighted an outer myoepithelial layer in some lobules. The lesion was classified B3 (indeterminate) without atypia.

The core biopsy findings were recorded as inconclusive and requiring clinicopathological and radiological interpretation in the context of sampling depth. A superficial sampling location was noted to favour a cutaneous adnexal tumour such as nodular hidradenoma, given the lobulated architecture and squamous differentiation; if the biopsied lesion originated from deeper breast tissue, a papilloma diagnosis was considered.

Malignancy was initially suspected on the basis of the radiological appearance (M5/U5) and patient age; this remained a documented initial working impression. The absence of cytological atypia and the lack of convincing breast acini supported the B3 classification without atypia, making invasive carcinoma less likely on the available sample.

The inconclusive biopsy findings were attributed in the record to likely sampling limitations in a heterogeneous lesion. The record states that surgical excision was required to establish a definitive diagnosis.

The radiological classification was reported as based on the most concerning features identified (focal reduced border definition on mammography and marked posterior acoustic shadowing on ultrasound) rather than the predominant overall morphology, with acknowledged possible interobserver variation.

Constructed selected-record review: this packet assembles findings recorded at different times (presentation, imaging, core biopsy and contemporaneous interpretation). The exact dates of each assessment, the number and gauge of core biopsy passes, the precise biopsy sampling depth relative to skin and breast parenchyma, and any second-review pathology opinion before excision are not reported in the supplied record and are therefore unknown. prepared_template.facts:

Patient: man in his 80s, past history of gout and prostate cancer (prostatectomy approximately 25 years ago, reported in remission). He presented to the emergency department after an episode of syncope, diagnosed as an upper respiratory infection, and was discharged on oral ciprofloxacin for 7 days. He re-presented after 5 days with recurrent syncope.

Rash history: a 2-month history of diffuse pruritic rash, treated with diphenhydramine, prednisone and famotidine with minimal improvement. All gout medications were discontinued at the onset of the rash 2 months ago. Symptoms remained the same after initiation of ciprofloxacin.

Examination at the emergency department visit: afebrile and haemodynamically stable, with pruritic erythematous indurated papules and scattered plaques on chest, lower abdomen, back and extremities.

Documented blood results at this presentation: haemoglobin 127 g/L, platelet count 169×10⁹/L, white blood count 7.2×10⁹/L, absolute monocyte count 2.6×10⁹/L, absolute eosinophil count 0.3×10⁹/L. Lactate dehydrogenase 379 U/L; uric acid level normal.

Skin biopsy result: superficial and deep perivascular and interstitial dermatitis with eosinophils, reported as consistent with a dermal hypersensitivity reaction, eosinophilic dermatosis of haematological malignancy (EDHM), or an early stage of an immune-mediated vesiculobullous disorder. These are recorded interpretations of the biopsy, not a confirmed diagnosis.

Recorded differential reasoning: DRESS syndrome was considered given eosinophilic cutaneous inflammation, but judged unlikely because of absence of recent exposure to a new high-risk medication, lack of fever, less facial involvement, no leucocytosis or eosinophilia, normal liver function tests and no evidence of internal organ involvement. The record states this 'further necessitated a workup for haematological malignancy'.

Flow cytometry from peripheral blood revealed expression of CD56 on monocytes. CT scan showed no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.

Documented management at discharge: the patient was discharged home with triamcinolone ointment and oral antihistamine medications. The record then states that he presented to haematology clinic after discharge, and that peripheral next-generation sequencing was obtained 'given the persistent monocytosis'. The results of that sequencing and any marrow findings are not available at this decision point.

Whether the monocytosis was sustained over time is therefore not established by the supplied data. No molecular, cytogenetic or bone marrow results are available at this decision point.

prepared_template.title: Discordant germ-cell tumour pathology with a new renal mass and venous thrombus
prepared_template.facts:
A man in his 40s with a history of childhood orchidopexy for cryptorchidism presented with 2 months of painful right hemiscrotal swelling, initially treated as epididymitis before re-presentation with persistent symptoms. Scrotal ultrasound showed diffuse heterogeneity of the right testicle with most of the testicle replaced by soft tissue mass. Staging CT of the abdomen and pelvis did not demonstrate metastatic disease. Initial serum markers: normal hCG, elevated AFP of 85 ng/mL and LDH of 257 U/L.

A resource constraint was documented at initial staging: CT of the chest was not obtained because insurance authorisation was not approved prior to pathological confirmation of malignancy; it was subsequently obtained after orchiectomy during oncology evaluation.

He underwent right inguinal radical orchiectomy. Initial histopathology reported an 8.3 cm pure seminoma with lymphovascular and epididymal invasion. Because of the elevated AFP, pathological review was requested; this identified a mixed germ cell tumour of approximately 95% seminoma and 5% postpubertal yolk sac tumour, pT2. The revised histology is documented; the discordance between the initial report and the marker remains part of the record.

Four cycles of etoposide and cisplatin (EP) were initially recommended. Due to his significant smoking history, bleomycin was not offered because of concern for pulmonary toxicity. Before chemotherapy could be initiated, treatment was delayed by an intervening infection.

One month after surgery, AFP increased to 280 ng/mL with normal hCG and LDH, without radiographic recurrence; he was deemed Stage IS per National Comprehensive Cancer Network criteria. Systemic chemotherapy with four cycles of EP was recommended due to the rising AFP. Prior to receiving chemotherapy, he presented to the emergency department with left flank pain and gross haematuria.

At the emergency department, urinalysis revealed significant blood and small bacteria but was otherwise within normal limits. AFP was 280 ng/mL with normal hCG and LDH. A non-contrast CT abdomen and pelvis revealed asymmetric left perirenal and periureteral oedema concerning for pyelonephritis and an enlarging indeterminate 4 mm left lower lobe nodule. He was discharged on antibiotics, and the planned EP chemotherapy was delayed because of the presumed infection.

Repeat contrast-enhanced imaging 1 month after the emergency department visit revealed new pulmonary nodules and a 9 cm mass in the upper pole of the left kidney with associated renal vein thrombosis. The thrombus could not be definitively characterised as tumour or bland and was considered indeterminate. Anticoagulation was not initiated due to ongoing gross haematuria. This is the assessment point: the renal mass, thrombus and haematuria are newly identified and tissue characterisation has not yet been obtained.

MRI characterisation of the renal lesion is recorded: an approximately 9 cm infiltrative mass involving the upper pole of the left kidney with extension into the interpolar region, renal sinus and collecting system, with associated left renal vein thrombosis.

The documented working differential for the flank pain and gross haematuria included urinary tract infection, nephrolithiasis, renal papillary necrosis and primary renal malignancy. The non-contrast CT findings initially favoured pyelonephritis; persistent AFP elevation after orchiectomy raised concern for active NSGCT despite previously negative staging imaging. These remain competing, unconfirmed explanations at this point.

Constructed selected-record review: this packet assembles findings acquired at different times (initial presentation, orchiectomy histopathology and its revision, the 1-month postoperative marker rise, the emergency department visit, and repeat imaging 1 month later). No single pretreatment time point contains all data. Data not reported in the supplied record at this decision point include platelet count, coagulation studies, formal chest staging results beyond the indeterminate nodule, and any tissue diagnosis of the renal mass; these are unknown, not normal.

prepared_template.title: Anorectal mucosal melanoma before definitive surgery
prepared_template.facts:
A man in his early 70s was referred for colonoscopy after several weeks of new-onset faecal urgency. He denied rectal bleeding, tenesmus, weight loss, abdominal pain or a change in stool calibre. There was no personal or family history of inflammatory bowel disease or colorectal cancer. Medical history included hypertension; he was an ex-smoker and a social alcohol consumer. Colonoscopy three years earlier for a change in bowel habit was reported as normal.

A faecal immunochemical test (FIT) requested in primary care was negative; faecal calprotectin was mildly elevated at 204 µg/g (local laboratory reference range <50 µg/g). A full infection screen was negative. He was taking no medication, including NSAIDs.

Colonoscopy was completed to the terminal ileum and showed a normal colon and terminal ileum, with no diverticular disease, mucosal inflammation or other polyps. On retroflexion, an 18 mm polypoid ulcerated lesion was identified arising at the anorectal junction; the lesion was pigmented on white light. It was not visible on forward (antegrade) view.

Biopsies revealed a cellular infiltrate within the bowel mucosa and submucosa composed of sheets of large ovoid cells with pleomorphic, hyperchromatic nuclei and prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemistry showed diffuse SOX10 positivity, confirming a melanocytic tumour and establishing the diagnosis of invasive mucosal melanoma. By mutational analysis the tumour was BRAF, KIT and NRAS wild-type, with a deletion of CDKN2A/2B present.

MRI of the pelvis was reported as showing the tumour contained within the rectal wall, with no evidence of peritoneal metastasis or pelvic lymphadenopathy, and no involvement of the internal or external anal sphincter. CT of the chest/abdomen/pelvis and PET-CT similarly demonstrated no evidence of nodal or distant metastatic disease.

To establish that this was a primary anorectal melanoma rather than a metastasis, the patient underwent assessment with full history, skin and ophthalmic examination. He had no prior history of cutaneous, ocular or mucosal melanoma. MRI of the pelvis showed no evidence of local or distant metastases and no other primary site of disease. The solitary mucosal lesion at the anorectal junction was therefore considered the primary tumour, recorded as staged T1 N0 M0.

Radiology is described as showing a 3.2 cm polypoid mass within the lower rectum arising on a stalk extending from the upper anal canal in the anterior midline.

The source contains conflicting accounts of sphincter involvement: the MRI account reports no involvement, whereas another imaging-based account states involvement. The original images, timing and basis of this discrepancy need clarification. No definitive resection choice is supplied.

prepared_template.title: Early recurrent bone tumour after a joint-preserving operation
prepared_template.facts:
An adolescent girl presented with gradually worsening pain and swelling around the lower left leg and ankle, with walking increasingly difficult over several months. There was no history of trauma, fever, weight loss or other systemic complaints. Examination showed diffuse swelling and tenderness over the distal tibia with painful restriction of ankle movement; distal circulation and neurological examination were normal.

Initial radiographs showed a well-defined expansile osteolytic lesion of the distal tibial metaphysis with cortical thinning and extension towards the subarticular region, without matrix calcification and with a relatively narrow zone of transition. A preoperative biopsy demonstrated histopathological features consistent with a giant cell tumour of bone.

At initial treatment, imaging and histopathology were interpreted as showing a primary giant cell tumour confined to the distal tibia without evidence of extraosseous extension. On that basis, a joint-preserving intralesional procedure was selected as the working approach. The patient underwent extended intralesional curettage with high-speed burr debridement of the cavity margins; the defect was reconstructed with autologous iliac crest bone graft and polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) cement using the sandwich technique. Postoperative radiographs showed satisfactory cavity filling with subchondral bone stock maintained.

Three months after surgery, the patient returned with recurrent pain and swelling. Repeat imaging showed recurrence of the lesion with proximal intramedullary extension, cortical destruction and soft-tissue involvement. The reported findings also included extension into the distal fibula. Clinically there was tense swelling over the distal leg and ankle with stretched overlying skin.

This is a constructed selected-record review. The record combines data acquired at different times: initial presentation, preoperative biopsy, first operation, and the three-month reassessment. The exact dates of each assessment, the patient's precise age, and the imaging modality used at recurrence beyond the described radiographic findings are not reported in the supplied material. No pretreatment time point beyond the described initial presentation is available.

Recorded availability limits relevant to the decision point: the source states that intraoperative frozen-section analysis to confirm tumour-free surgical margins was not performed before definitive reconstruction in this case, and that histopathological confirmation of negative margins before reconstruction is preferable whenever feasible. Whether frozen-section analysis is available at the clinician's own institution is not established by this record.

Background context from the source: giant cell tumour of bone is histologically benign but frequently behaves in a locally destructive manner; distal tibial involvement is relatively rare and difficult to manage because the lesion lies close to the ankle joint. Extended curettage remains preferred for many lesions, but aggressive tumours may recur despite appropriate surgery, and recurrent disease around the distal tibia may require wide excision and complex reconstruction associated with complications including graft failure, instability and limb shortening.

The source also records, as general context rather than patient-specific data, that recurrence rates of 10% to 25% following curettage have been reported, particularly in lesions with cortical destruction and soft-tissue extension, and that wide excision may be necessary in recurrent or aggressive lesions to achieve adequate local control.

Candidate essential information requirement 1 (proposed, not a documented decision): cross-sectional imaging (MRI of the distal tibia and fibula, with CT as a clinically equivalent alternative) to define the full proximal intramedullary extent, the soft-tissue component and confirmed distal fibular involvement before any resection margin planning. Justification: the presentation documents proximal spread, cortical destruction and soft-tissue involvement, and the choice between repeat intralesional surgery and wide excision depends on the true anatomical extent. Timing: before the next surgical decision. Practical source: local radiology department.

Candidate essential information requirement 2 (proposed, not a documented decision): tissue confirmation of the recurrent lesion and, if resection proceeds, intraoperative frozen-section or definitive histopathological margin assessment. Justification: the record documents that frozen-section margin confirmation was not performed in this case and states that histopathological confirmation of negative margins before definitive reconstruction is preferable whenever feasible; whether the recurrence represents residual versus new disease and whether margins are clear directly affect the local control decision. Timing: biopsy of the recurrence before surgery, and margin assessment at surgery. Practical source: local pathology service; if frozen section is unavailable, planned delayed definitive reconstruction until permanent margins are reported is a clinically equivalent alternative.

Scope notes for the later answering task: D5b (evidence-sensitive belief updating) and D6c (sycophancy resistance) are out of scope for this static written task. D4b (trend detection) is assessable through the documented change from an apparently contained lesion at initial imaging to proximal extension, cortical destruction and soft-tissue involvement at three months. D6a (escalation) is assessable only insofar as the three-month recurrence with soft-tissue involvement constitutes a current clinical problem requiring prompt reassessment; historical illness alone does not establish current acute deterioration. All other listed behaviours should be scored if assessable; missing requested behaviour is low performance, not N/A.

prepared_template.title: New facial destruction after advanced skin cancer treatment
prepared_template.facts:
A man in his 70s with a history of allergic rhinitis, chronic left-sided hearing loss and long-term tobacco use presented to the emergency department with 3 days of worsening right-sided facial pain after hearing a 'popping' sound while inserting dentures. He was retired, lived alone and maintained only intermittent contact with family. He reported difficulty obtaining health insurance, unstable transportation and limited social support. No formal mental health evaluation or psychiatric diagnosis was documented in his medical record.

His dermatologic history began approximately two decades earlier with Mohs surgery for a basal cell carcinoma (BCC) of the right temple. In his mid-60s, he noticed a 'shaving nick' on the right upper lip that evolved into a chronic ulcer; care was delayed due to lack of insurance. A shave biopsy in early 2019 confirmed recurrent nodular BCC, but planned surgical resection was postponed because of ongoing insurance problems and he was lost to follow-up.

In 2021, he re-presented with a rapidly enlarging midfacial lesion. Cross-sectional imaging revealed an extensive ulcerative mass involving the right maxilla with cavitation, soft tissue thickening and bony destruction. PET-CT identified intense FDG uptake in the primary tumour and a separate FDG-avid posterior thoracic nodule. He began systemic therapy with vismodegib, then later transitioned to cemiplimab due to progression. Proton radiotherapy was recommended to maximise preservation of the orbit and central nervous system structures, and he completed this with the expected acute toxicities.

The 2021 systemic treatments were vismodegib 150 mg orally once daily, then cemiplimab 350 mg intravenously every 3 weeks after multidisciplinary review, each given over about 2 months (total treatment length approximately 4 months). He completed curative-intent proton therapy to 70 GyRBE in 35 fractions, with expected acute toxicities managed conservatively.

Imaging in late 2021 and early 2022 showed a large, persistent post-treatment defect with destruction of the maxilla, hard palate and orbital floor but no definite evidence of recurrence. Transportation barriers prevented planned reconstructive surgery. Records from 2023 indicated monitoring of yet another new lesion but did not show evidence of active intervention.

A PET-CT in 2024 demonstrated stable post-treatment changes, improved metabolic activity and no metastases. In mid-2025, he developed sudden facial pain and worsening deformity. On presentation, he had difficulty speaking, swallowing and maintaining oral intake due to structural instability of the midface.

Head and neck CT at the 2025 presentation showed a large soft tissue defect of the right midface with bony destruction of the anterior wall and antrum of the right maxillary sinus including portions of the right maxillary alveolar ridge and right hard palate, complete opacification of the right frontal sinus, partial opacification of the right maxillary sinus antrum and the absence of numerous teeth. Findings also included a new soft tissue ulceration extending inferiorly along the mid and right mandibular region, concerning for disease recurrence, with associated erosive changes of the adjacent mandible and likely acute pathologic fracture of the right hemimandibular body.

CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis demonstrated findings concerning for distant metastases: multiple pulmonary nodules and masses scattered throughout both lungs, lytic lesions with cortical erosions in the right sixth rib and left eighth through tenth ribs, and multifocal irregular hypodense hepatic masses. Liver MRI showed multiple hepatic masses, the largest in segment 8 measuring 3.5 cm anteriorly with delayed central enhancement, isointense lesions in segments 3, 6 and 7, and three indeterminate hypoenhancing hepatic foci. No suspicious lymphadenopathy was visualised.

Recorded initial considerations at the 2025 presentation (documented as provisional differential reasoning, not confirmed conclusions): given his history of high-dose proton radiotherapy, osteoradionecrosis was an important initial consideration, and the abrupt 'popping' sensation with exposed bone and mandibular instability was consistent with a post-radiation pathologic fracture; however, the new enlarging soft tissue ulceration extending beyond the prior radiation field raised concern for recurrent malignancy rather than a purely radiation-related injury. Superinfection of a chronic ulcer was also considered, as the patient reported increasing pain and functional decline, although infection would not account for the rapid progression of tissue destruction seen on imaging. An alternative primary head and neck malignancy was also evaluated as a possibility.

Constructed selected-record review: this packet assembles source facts recorded at different times (2019, 2021, 2023, 2024 and the 2025 admission). At the stated decision point, the results of punch biopsy of the new mandibular ulceration and of hepatic lesion biopsy, the tumour board's determination, and any subsequent treatment decisions or outcomes are not supplied and are unknown to this record. Unreported information is unknown, not normal; no pretreatment time point beyond the documented 2025 presentation is implied.

Practical constraints documented in the record: lack of insurance delayed the initial 2019 care; insurance instability prevented definitive surgical excision; transportation barriers prevented planned reconstructive surgery after 2021 treatment; the patient lives alone with intermittent family contact and limited social support. These constraints are part of the documented history and bear on feasibility of any proposed plan.

prepared_template.title: Progressive urinary tract disease despite repeated empirical diagnoses
prepared_template.facts:
A male in his late 50s has had recurrent lower urinary tract symptoms over approximately 6 years, initially managed as benign prostatic hyperplasia and later as tuberculous cystitis. Despite multiple courses of medical therapy and limited surgical approaches, symptoms persisted, and repeat imaging and cystoscopy showed progressive bladder wall thickening extending to the prostate and distal ureters. He was readmitted for further evaluation after failure of conservative and medical management.

Approximately five years before the final admission, he had persistent lower urinary tract symptoms without systemic symptoms. Ultrasound showed prostatic enlargement with normal prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels. Cystoscopy showed an enlarged, high-walled prostate with grossly normal mucosa, and transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) was performed. Histopathology demonstrated benign prostatic hyperplasia with chronic prostatitis.

Approximately four years before the final admission, he presented with gross haematuria. Repeat cystoscopy and TURP revealed petechial haemorrhages along the bladder wall and fibrotic changes in the prostate. Histopathology showed non-caseating granulomas with Langhans and foreign body-type giant cells.

Approximately three years before the final admission, cystoscopy revealed areas of bladder wall thickening and transurethral resection of the bladder (TURBT) was performed. Histopathology revealed xanthogranulomatous cystitis, including areas of caseating and non-caseating granulomas with Langhans and foreign body type multinucleated giant cells. HIV screening was negative. Urine culture and urine TB RT-PCR were negative; however, the attending specialist empirically treated him for extra-pulmonary tuberculous cystitis, and he completed standard anti-tuberculosis therapy (2HRZE/4HR).

Within 2 years before the final admission, dysuria and pyuria persisted. Surveillance cystoscopy showed progressive bladder wall thickening with yellowish bases and petechial changes on the prostate. Antibiotic therapy yielded only minimal relief. Three months before the final admission, MRI of the lumbosacral spine was unremarkable except for left hydroureteric changes. Urine studies revealed sterile pyuria, prompting admission for definitive management.

At the current reassessment, the documented working diagnosis was xanthogranulomatous cystoprostatitis with a possible tuberculous component, given prior histologic and clinical findings. Differential diagnoses, although not strongly considered, included urothelial carcinoma of the bladder or prostate, primary genitourinary tuberculosis and chronic bacterial prostatitis. This working diagnosis remains provisional.

On the current admission, cystoscopy revealed diffuse yellowish thickening across the bladder and a markedly trabeculated, non-distensible bladder with a capacity of 40–50 mL, with similar involvement of the prostate. Given significant tissue and function loss of the bladder, radical cystoprostatectomy with ileal conduit was offered to the patient, to which the patient agreed.

Recorded evidence limits: the source reports negative urine culture and urine TB RT-PCR at the time of the third procedure, and sterile pyuria on later urine studies, but does not report repeated mycobacterial cultures, interferon-gamma release assays, acid-fast staining, or upper-tract imaging beyond the noted left hydroureteric change on lumbosacral MRI. Malignancy exclusion rests on prior resection histopathology; no dedicated staging imaging or repeat biopsy at the current admission is reported in the supplied record. Unreported data are unknown, not normal.

This is a constructed selected-record review: the findings above were acquired at different times over approximately six years, and the record does not provide a single uniform pretreatment time point. The assessment point is the current reassessment before any radical surgery; later radical specimen findings, final extent of inflammation, postoperative function and symptom outcome are withheld and must not be assumed.

prepared_template.title: Acute abdominal signs with massive proteinuria but no overt oedema
prepared_template.facts:
A boy under 10 years old with no reported medical history presented with severe abdominal pain and repeated vomiting since the previous evening. Temperature 36.9°C, blood pressure 103/54 mm Hg, pulse 119 beats/min.

Examination showed abdominal distension, right lower quadrant tenderness and rebound tenderness, without oedema or purpura.

Abdominal radiography showed dilated, gas-filled small-bowel loops. Ultrasonography showed a keyboard sign in a dilated small-bowel loop (diameter 15 mm; wall thickness 3.7 mm), with to-and-fro movement on supplemental video.

The ultrasonographic inferior vena cava-to-aorta ratio (IVC/Ao) was 0.4, below the 0.8 cut-off indicating intravascular volume depletion.

Laboratory findings: white blood cells 13.5×10⁹/L; haemoglobin 140 g/L; haematocrit 0.42 L/L; albumin 2.0 g/dL; BUN 11.5 mg/dL; creatinine 0.3 mg/dL (BUN/Cr ratio 38.3); Na 139 mEq/L; K 4.5 mEq/L; Cl 106 mEq/L; total cholesterol 204 mg/dL; triglycerides 30 mg/dL; C3 148 mg/dL; C4 30 mg/dL; D-dimer 1.3 µg/mL (normal <1.0 µg/mL); fibrinogen 544 mg/dL.

Urinalysis revealed high specific gravity. Massive proteinuria was confirmed by a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) of 27.1 g/g creatinine, without haematuria.

Recorded context: the keyboard sign and to-and-fro movement are described as characteristic ultrasonographic findings of small bowel obstruction, and the keyboard sign is described as suggestive of small bowel obstruction.

Availability limits: this is a constructed selected-record review at the initial assessment point. No documented initial working diagnosis is recorded in the supplied material at this point. prepared_template.title: Persistent chylous mediastinal drainage when embolisation cannot be completed
prepared_template.facts:
A woman in her early 40s underwent stand-alone subaortic membrane resection with limited septal myectomy via full median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass. Limited rather than extensive myectomy was chosen because of a relatively thin septal thickness of 1.1 cm. Intraoperatively, excessive mediastinal adipose tissue and suspected thymic hyperplasia were encountered, requiring meticulous dissection with electrocautery and haemostatic clips. Neither pleural cavity was entered. Anterior and posterior mediastinal 24 Fr Blake drains and temporary pacing wires were placed before standard sternal closure. There were no intraoperative complications, and immediate postoperative echocardiography showed the peak LVOT gradient reduced to 14 mm Hg with preserved valvular function.

Relevant comorbidity recorded before surgery: obesity (body mass index 45 kg/m²), chronic tobacco use, vaping, hypothyroidism, hyperlipidaemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus and obstructive sleep apnoea. She had been diagnosed with the subaortic membrane approximately 10 years earlier and managed conservatively while asymptomatic; over the year before surgery she developed exertional dyspnoea and NYHA class III symptoms with increasing LVOT gradients, peak gradients nearly 70 mm Hg on follow-up echocardiography.

On postoperative day 2, after resumption of oral intake, the mediastinal drainage changed from serosanguineous to milky, with output of approximately 400–550 mL over 24 hours. Chylomediastinum was suspected on the basis of the fluid appearance and its timing after oral intake. After this suspected diagnosis, the chest tubes were transitioned from wall suction to water seal for passive drainage with close output monitoring.

Biochemical analysis of the milky drainage confirmed chylomediastinum, with triglyceride levels of 1095 mg/dL (normal <110 mg/dL; diagnostic threshold >110 mg/dL for chylous fluid). Baseline chest radiography and echocardiography showed no pericardial effusion, tamponade or additional drainable mediastinal collections.

Initial conservative management consisted of nil per os status and total parenteral nutrition to reduce chyle production; however, chest tube output remained persistently elevated at approximately 400–500 mL per day.

On postoperative day 8, interventional radiology performed an intranodal lymphangiogram using Lipiodol (ethiodised oil) to evaluate thoracic duct anatomy and identify the site of lymphatic leakage. The study showed contrast extravasation and pooling along the superior mediastinal lymphatic chain, without evidence of a discrete thoracic duct injury. Despite visualisation of mediastinal lymphatics, multiple attempts at thoracic duct cannulation and embolisation were unsuccessful. Given the technical difficulty and the absence of a clearly identifiable embolisation target, further interventional attempts were not pursued.

The lymphangiogram was interpreted as showing pooling of contrast and opacification of the superior mediastinal lymphatic chain on the left side, along the cranial portion of the anterior mediastinal drain.

Alternative causes of milky drainage were reported as considered and judged unlikely: infected or purulent drainage and empyema, given no clinical or radiographic evidence of infection and no pleural entry; lipid-containing drainage unrelated to lymphatic injury, given lymphangiographic extravasation; pseudochylous effusion, given the acute postoperative presentation; and residual haemostatic or topical surgical material, given onset only after resumption of oral intake with persistent milky appearance. Chylomediastinum was the favoured diagnosis because drainage became milky after oral intake, triglyceride was markedly elevated, and intranodal lymphangiography demonstrated mediastinal lymphatic extravasation.

Constructed selected-record review and availability limits: this packet assembles recorded facts from the published case up to the stated decision point (postoperative day 8, after the unsuccessful cannulation attempt). Data were documented at different times and some information is not reported at this point: serial daily drain outputs beyond the approximate 400–500 mL/day figure, trends in nutritional markers, electrolyte or immune status, body weight, fever or white cell count, and the exact technical details of why cannulation failed are not supplied. prepared_template.title: Discharge planning with differing accounts of home support
prepared_template.facts:
A man was admitted to the Frailty Assessment Unit. The admission social history records a once-daily package of care for medication prompts.

Nursing staff handed the patient over to the medical team on the basis that he was deaf. Staff who had interacted with him said he could lip read sufficiently if spoken to slowly and clearly, but that he was also a BSL user. The phrase 'lip reads' was documented multiple times in the clerk-in document, although the BSL user box was not ticked on the front of the admission booklet. How his lip-reading ability was assessed could not be ascertained from the clerk-in, but it was accepted by staff as sufficient for communication.

On day 3 the patient was seen on the ward round by a Consultant Geriatrician and a Resident Doctor. After that consultation it was decided that he was ready for home, to be discharged with his existing package of care. This decision was based on the patient supposedly lip reading what staff were saying and replying with nodding for yes and shaking his head for no; he agreed to most questions asked of him.

A resident doctor returned to the patient after the ward round to confirm some answers using basic British Sign Language. The Consultant had asked whether his package of care was three times a day and included washing and meals, and the patient had nodded in agreement; when asked with BSL this was found to be incorrect.

Through basic BSL it was found that the package of care was only once a day and that he had no family close by to regularly support him. Basic BSL was also used to confirm whether he currently had any pain and whether he had other questions at that time. After this consultation and discussion with the team, the resident doctor informed the patient that he would not be discharged that day.

When past correspondence was reviewed on the online clinical portal, recent clinic letters stated that the patient required a BSL interpreter for all consultations. This was raised with the Consultant, who said that lip reading was sufficient and no BSL interpreter was required.

During admission, staff had tried to use written materials to communicate with the patient, despite online clinic letters recording that he struggled to read written English and could not effectively write due to a severe bilateral tremor. He also had several ophthalmology letters stating poor eyesight due to chronic ophthalmological conditions, further contra-indicating written media. The patient conveyed that he preferred not to communicate in writing, yet staff persisted in attempting that mode.

Up until this point (day 3), at no time during admission had a professional interpreter been offered or requested. The medical team contacted the patient's next of kin (a fellow BSL user, although not deaf), who usually took on the role of interpreting for the patient; over the phone he confirmed that the patient was a BSL user.

Sign language, not spoken or written English, was the patient's primary form of communication.

At this decision point, no professional interpreter had been requested or offered during the first three days of admission, and the reliability of lip-reading had not been established. Basic BSL communication on day 3 indicated once-daily contact and no nearby family support. The full type and scope of home support had not been established through a professional-interpreter-assisted discussion. The basic BSL account conflicts with the account obtained through nodding during the ward round.

cases.title: Acute respiratory failure during several cancer treatments

Background and treatment exposure
A man in his 80s has non-rheumatic aortic stenosis and metastatic HER2-positive distal oesophageal adenocarcinoma. His regimen includes pembrolizumab, trastuzumab and FOLFOX. Pembrolizumab 200 mg every three weeks began nine weeks before admission; three doses had been given, the last 14 days before this presentation. prepared_template.title: Acute respiratory failure during several cancer treatments
prepared_template.facts:
Background and treatment exposure
A man in his 80s has non-rheumatic aortic stenosis and metastatic HER2-positive distal oesophageal adenocarcinoma. His regimen includes pembrolizumab, trastuzumab and FOLFOX. Pembrolizumab 200 mg every three weeks began nine weeks before admission; three doses had been given, the last 14 days before this presentation. Cycle 5 day 1 of FOLFOX plus trastuzumab was given the day before admission. A continuous 46-hour fluorouracil infusion was still running when he presented. The first four cycles were reported as well tolerated apart from mild peripheral oedema attributed to dexamethasone premedication.

Acute presentation
Rapidly progressive dyspnoea developed overnight, with wheeze and orthopnoea. He denied chest pain, fever, cough and worsening peripheral oedema. Pulse was 107/min, respiratory rate 31/min, BP 156/85 mmHg and oxygen saturation 87% on room air. He required CPAP and supplemental oxygen at 10 L/min.

Available investigations
Initial high-sensitivity troponin was 11,374 ng/L (reference 3–35), whole-blood lactate 4.4 mmol/L, NT-proBNP 3,975 pg/mL and D-dimer 928 ng/mL. Venous pH was 7.30 and pCO2 51 mmHg. Initial ECG showed a chronic left bundle branch block without new ischaemic changes. CTPA reported no pulmonary embolus, diffuse pulmonary oedema and scattered subsegmental air-space opacities favoured to be atelectatic change.

In the emergency department he received bronchodilators, aspirin, sublingual nitroglycerin, empirical ceftriaxone and azithromycin, intravenous furosemide and intravenous heparin for a presumed non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Troponin subsequently reached 34,066 ng/L approximately 13 hours after presentation. The ECG figure caption describes new T-wave inversions in V2–V3 and possible evolving changes in V4–V6 between early recordings, while the narrative describes no dynamic ischaemic changes. prepared_template.title: Respiratory arrest with evolving autonomic and neurological findings
prepared_template.facts:
Presentation and progression
A man in his 40s with longstanding schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes was admitted after an unwitnessed collapse at home. He had reduced alertness and could not follow commands; the initial neurological examination was otherwise unremarkable. Two days after admission he became unstable with fever and respiratory arrest, requiring intubation and ventilation.

By approximately day 10 he remained ventilator-dependent. He could follow simple commands but attention fluctuated. Bradycardia, apnoeas, intermittent fever without an identified infectious correlate, anisocoria and labile BP were documented; isoprenaline and a temporary pacing wire were needed in intensive care. Examination now showed slow horizontal saccades, limited upgaze, spasticity, brisk reflexes, limb clonus, extensor plantar responses and right laterocollis.

Available investigation reports
Routine initial blood results were described as unremarkable except CK 3,120 U/L (reference below 320). CTPA showed a small subsegmental pulmonary embolus. Chest radiography did not show pneumothorax. During ventilation, gas-exchange measures and the A–a gradient were described as within normal limits. Numerical ventilator/gas measurements are not reproduced.

Brain MRI showed bilateral mesial temporal and posterior left thalamic T2-FLAIR high signal. Spinal MRI was normal. CSF contained 30 white cells, 99% lymphocytes, protein 0.55 g/L and glucose 5.1 mmol/L, with IgG index 1.92 (reference below 0.7) and CSF-exclusive oligoclonal bands. The report describes no identified infectious organisms; a complete dated microbiology panel is not reproduced. EEG showed generalised slowing without epileptiform features.

An initial autoimmune encephalitis panel in serum and CSF was reported as negative apart from low-positive GAD65 in serum, undetectable in CSF. The complete panel membership is not supplied here. CT thorax/abdomen/pelvis and whole-body PET-CT were unremarkable, but testicular ultrasound described a heterogeneous left testis with microcalcifications. No tissue diagnosis is provided.

Record limits
The exact ordering of all imaging, CSF and antibody tests is not established. The full medication list, exposure history and timing of any immunotherapy relative to these tests are not supplied. A woman in her 40s had biopsy-proven sarcoidosis with cardiac and pulmonary involvement three years before this admission. Over approximately 12 months she lost 21 kg, reported as 34.4% of baseline weight; 11 kg of the loss occurred during the last six months. She has marked sarcopenia, weakness, secondary amenorrhoea and iron-deficiency anaemia. She has hyperpigmented macules and a pepper-and-salt rash described as compatible with cutaneous sarcoidosis. A comprehensive immunological panel was unremarkable. ACE reached 62 U/L (reference 12–55). A Synacthen test was reported as excluding adrenal insufficiency. Nasal endoscopy was unremarkable. Brain MRI showed no abnormal enhancement; EEG and lumbar puncture were reported as normal, with no focal neurological deficit. Whole-body CT did not identify active systemic sarcoidosis or another explanation. Psychiatric assessment did not support an eating disorder, although a first-degree relative had anorexia nervosa.

prepared_template.title: Plaques and sensory abnormalities during treatment for CLL
prepared_template.facts:
History and exposure context
A man in his 50s from North India has CLL diagnosed six months earlier and is taking acalabrutinib 100 mg twice daily. For two months he has had mildly pruritic, erythematous, scaly plaques on the trunk and limbs. He did not report sensory or motor deficits during the history.

Objective examination
There are multiple well-defined infiltrated dusky erythematous scaly plaques, from 0.5 × 0.5 cm to 8 × 5 cm, over the neck, trunk and limbs. Examination finds approximately 50% sensory loss over plaques, infiltrated earlobes and glove-pattern sensory loss in both hands without motor weakness. Both ulnar and common peroneal nerves are thickened, firm and non-tender. There is no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Nerve-conduction testing reports sensory neuropathy in both upper limbs.

Available laboratory and tissue findings
Haemoglobin is 104 g/L, white-cell count 33 × 10^9/L and platelets 92 × 10^9/L; other routine results are described as within normal limits. Dermoscopy shows red-purple dots/globules and white scale on a red-brown background.

Skin biopsy shows focal parakeratosis, irregular acanthosis and multifocal spongiosis. There is an upper-dermal band-like infiltrate containing epithelioid granulomas with a peripheral lymphocyte rim, and granulomatous infiltrates around vessels and adnexa in the middle/deep dermis. Fite-Faraco staining does not reveal organisms. Immunohistochemistry shows abundant CD3-positive T cells, more CD4-positive than CD8-positive, with a minor CD20-positive B-cell component described as reactive/polytypic rather than a monoclonal leukaemic infiltrate. Slit-skin smears from two back plaques and both earlobes are negative.

Record limits
The duration or progression of the objectively detected sensory deficit is not established by the patient’s initial denial. A detailed exposure/contact history, dated baseline neurological map, additional microbiological assessment and a complete drug-interaction/bleeding assessment are not supplied. No final diagnostic label, selected treatment, oncological clearance or later nerve/skin response is provided.

prepared_template.title: Progressive sleep disorder with incomplete antibody evidence
prepared_template.facts:
A man in his 60s with no previous neurological disease has had progressive sleep–wake dysregulation with hypersomnolence and associated cognitive impairment evolving over 36 months. The earliest symptoms were excessive daytime sleepiness with prolonged, unplanned daytime naps, often followed by episodes of confusion.

Approximately 5 months after symptom onset he was involved in a major road traffic accident that was most likely sleep-related, causing acute kidney injury from rhabdomyolysis requiring renal replacement therapy in intensive care. Brain MRI during that admission was unremarkable and intermittent confusion was present.

After discharge he was diagnosed with obstructive sleep apnoea with an oxygen desaturation index (over 4%) of 27 per hour; body mass index was normal at 23 kg/m2. Continuous positive airway pressure was started at 13 months after symptom onset but was later discontinued by the patient, who reported perceived resolution of symptoms.

He then developed vivid visual hallucinations, sleep episodes lasting up to 36–48 hours, and abnormal nocturnal behaviours including apparent dream enactment and complex motor activity; he was not on any medication to attribute these symptoms. Cognition gradually deteriorated, affecting short-term memory, attention and executive function; recognition of close relatives was preserved initially but became impaired over time. There was no history of dysarthria, dysphagia, stridor, clinical parkinsonism or reported personality change.

Neurological examination at 32 months of symptom onset showed intact cranial nerve function, normal facial expressions and speech, and no gaze palsy. Motor examination demonstrated normal tone, power and reflexes. There were no rigidity, tremor, bradykinesia or frontal release signs. Gait and postural stability were preserved.

Serum encephalitis panel: anti-IgLON5 antibodies positive (1:1000; reference negative, with any detectable antibodies considered positive). Anti-LGI1, CASPR2, NMDA receptor, DPPX, glycine receptor, AMPA2, GABA-B receptor and Hu, Yo, Ri antibodies were all negative. C-reactive protein was persistently elevated.

CSF findings: white blood cells <3×10⁶/L (normal); protein 0.5 g/L (normal); oligoclonal bands negative. A panel of neuronal antibodies in CSF (NMDA receptor, LGI1, DPPX, Hu, Yo, Ri) was reported negative. Orexin/hypocretin was not analysable. CSF anti-IgLON5 antibodies were NOT tested, because the sample was not received by the laboratory; this is unperformed testing, not a negative result.

Imaging: MRI brain showed no focal inflammatory or neoplastic lesions and no focal cortical or brainstem atrophy; mild non-specific deep white matter hyperintensities (centrum semiovale and corona radiata) and a small old incidental cerebellar infarct. CT thorax, abdomen and pelvis showed no evidence of malignancy. FDG PET-CT was non-diagnostic because of significant patient movement during acquisition.

Electroencephalogram showed mild diffuse symmetrical background slowing with preserved posterior dominant rhythm reactivity and no epileptiform discharges. Polysomnography at 38 months showed marked sleep fragmentation, continuous stereotyped movements and oneiric behaviours, difficulty staging sleep, and no clear REM sleep architecture.

Cognitive testing (Addenbrooke's Cognitive Assessment III): at 29 months total 75 (attention 12/18, memory 19/26, fluency 4/14, language 24/26, visuospatial 16/16); at 36 months total 71 (attention 13/18, memory 12/26, fluency 5/14, language 25/26, visuospatial 16/16), with memory decline between the two assessments.

The diagnosis recorded at this review is anti-IgLON5 encephalitis, based on the clinical phenotype and serum antibody titre of 1:1000 at 36 months after symptom onset. CSF anti-IgLON5 testing was not performed because the sample was not received. No tissue-level confirmation is supplied. No treatment or treatment response is provided at this decision point.

Availability limits for this review: the exact dates of the serum panel, CSF studies, MRI, CT, PET-CT and EEG are not individually documented; polysomnography post-dates the 36-month diagnostic label; orexin/hypocretin was not analysable; CSF IgLON5 testing was not performed; and PET-CT was non-diagnostic for technical reasons. Unreported data are unknown, not normal.

prepared_template.title: Confirmed periampullary cancer with biliary obstruction during pregnancy
prepared_template.facts:
Presentation and pregnancy
A woman in her mid-20s, gravida 2 para 1 with no known comorbidity, presented at 25 weeks’ gestation with epigastric pain, nausea, occasional vomiting and mild pruritus. The pain was non-colicky, non-radiating, unrelated to food and partly relieved by oral analgesics. Her previous pregnancy ended by caesarean at 34 weeks for fetal distress. Examination found mild jaundice and epigastric tenderness; she was afebrile and haemodynamically stable.

Available blood and ultrasound results
Haemoglobin was 83 g/L, WBC 9.1 × 10^9/L and platelets 430 × 10^9/L. Total/direct bilirubin were 4.4/2.8 mg/dL, ALT 50 U/L, AST 33 U/L and ALP 227 U/L. CA19-9 and CEA were within normal limits. Ultrasound showed common bile duct diameter 22 mm, dilated intrahepatic ducts, microlithiasis and gallbladder sludge.

Confirmed lesion and anatomical reports
Gastroduodenoscopy found a noduloproliferative lesion in the second duodenal segment causing approximately 50% luminal narrowing. Endoscopic ultrasound showed a large heteroechoic periampullary mass with upstream biliary dilatation. Biopsies confirmed adenocarcinoma.

Non-contrast MRI described asymmetric 2–2.5 cm thickening of the distal second/third duodenal segments with ulcerated margins and periduodenal soft-tissue change, without gastric outlet obstruction. The distal common bile duct was involved with severe narrowing; the proximal duct measured 2.5 cm. The pancreatic duct was not dilated. The lesion abutted the head/uncinate pancreas and small periduodenal nodes were reported. These observations do not provide final operative or pathological staging. The MRI documented a live intrauterine pregnancy at 25+5 weeks in cephalic presentation.

Current boundary
She was referred to the receiving institution at 27 weeks. Serial bilirubin, current maternal symptoms/infection assessment, current fetal growth/well-being, detailed resectability review, patient preferences and an agreed treatment/delivery plan are not supplied. No later procedure success, treatment response, delivery indication or outcome is provided. Malignancy is already biopsy-confirmed; the task is not to infer whether cancer exists.

prepared_template.facts:
Background and long course
A man in his late 70s has hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, Barrett’s oesophagus, a moderate sliding hiatal hernia, severe sigmoid diverticulosis and benign prostatic hyperplasia. He has not had abdominal surgery. Free intraperitoneal air was first documented approximately six years before this review while he was asymptomatic. A CT approximately nine years earlier showed no free air. Approximately five years earlier, CT showed free air, small-bowel pneumatosis and a small amount of pelvic fluid without surrounding inflammatory change. He remained clinically stable without an operation.

Symptoms and current examination
Abdominal swelling began approximately four years before review and evolved into daily bloating, early satiety and pain when unable to pass gas, relieved by passing gas. He denied vomiting. Small drinks or meals could trigger symptoms, and stools were unusually large and hard. He reports symptom relief with kefir, psyllium and tea; this is a patient-reported association. He also reports exertional dyspnoea/fatigue after approximately two miles of walking. Current and previous examinations describe a distended tympanic abdomen without rebound, guarding or rigidity, with stable vital signs.

Selected recent investigations
A lung-screening chest CT showed large-volume pneumoperitoneum, a partly imaged right retroperitoneal gas/fluid collection versus distended descending duodenum, and small-volume lower-oesophageal pneumomediastinum. About one month later, contrast CT abdomen/pelvis showed persistent large pneumoperitoneum, a duodenal diverticulum and a right anterior perirenal contrast collection potentially communicating near the D1/D2 junction. The report did not identify bowel wall discontinuity, wall thickening, fat stranding or abscess.

Colonoscopies about five years earlier and one month after the recent presentation showed severe sigmoid diverticular disease, otherwise normal colon. Upper endoscopies about two years earlier and one month after presentation showed Barrett’s and a moderate hiatal hernia without ulceration or visible perforation.

Record limits
The actual original images are not supplied, and a fistulous communication, active leak or a single source of the free air has not been established in this packet. A woman in her mid-20s presented to the emergency department with a 4-day history of headache and cervical pain accompanied by paraesthesia in the right upper extremity, followed by 2 days of progressive right-sided weakness. She reported difficulty performing fine motor tasks and intermittent febrile episodes. C-reactive protein and other inflammatory markers were also elevated.

Recorded limits of the available data at this point: the head CT excluded acute intracranial pathology only; no spinal imaging had been performed. Culture results from blood and urine were pending at the decision point and are not reported here. prepared_template.title: Congenital eye disease with infection-like systemic findings
prepared_template.facts:
A female infant was born at 30 weeks' gestation with a birth weight of 0.945 kg to a non-consanguineous couple of Indian ancestry. Parents reported a whitish appearance of both eyes since birth and a history of intraventricular haemorrhage that resolved after birth. Antenatal scan reportedly showed intrauterine growth retardation with increased cerebral flow and low foetal movement.

Ocular examination under anaesthesia showed bilateral buphthalmia with horizontal corneal diameters of 13 mm (right eye) and 12.5 mm (left eye), grade 2 corneal haze in both eyes and no lenticular opacity. Intraocular pressure was 21 mm Hg in the right eye and 19 mm Hg in the left eye. B-scan ultrasound was normal in both eyes.

She was diagnosed with bilateral congenital glaucoma and underwent combined trabeculotomy and trabeculectomy in both eyes. At 6 weeks' follow-up, corneal clarity had improved, the lens was clear, cup-disc ratio was 0.6 in both eyes and IOP was controlled. Retinopathy of prematurity screening showed mature retina bilaterally.

Over the next 6 months, IOP rose to 28 mm Hg in the right eye and 19 mm Hg in the left eye, and topical antiglaucoma medications were started in both eyes. Fundus examination showed a 0.9 cup-disc ratio in the right eye and 0.6 in the left eye.

Systemic evaluation documented global developmental delay, encephalopathy, high arched palate, long philtrum, hepatosplenomegaly, increased muscle tone, brisk reflexes, hypothyroidism, poor feed intake and moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss confirmed on brainstem evoked response audiometry. She was referred to a paediatric neurologist, who advised MRI of the brain.

MRI brain showed severe ventriculomegaly with rounded frontal horns and calcifications in the lenticulostriate vessels. There was diffuse T2 hyperintensity of the white matter with maximal rarefaction in the temporal, frontal and parietal lobes, increased apparent diffusion coefficient and cystic changes on FLAIR. The cerebral hemispheres were atrophic with gyral simplification. There was a large cisterna magna, T2 hyperintensity of the internal and external capsules, deep cerebellar white matter and middle cerebellar peduncles, severe pontine and middle cerebellar peduncle atrophy, and marked thinning of the corpus callosum and optic nerves, while the cerebellum remained well formed.

CSF analysis showed normal 5-methyltetrahydrofolate levels and significantly elevated neopterin with normal biopterin and very low biopterin percentage of total pterins. TORCH serology was negative except for high CMV IgG (6.904 AU/mL); however, PCR on blood and urine were negative. The mother's CMV IgG was simultaneously elevated at 3.92 AU/mL. Liver enzymes were mildly elevated (SGOT 47, GGT 82, LDH 383 U/L).

At this stage of the record, the clinicians recorded three principal differential diagnoses for the combination of congenital glaucoma, encephalopathy, intracranial calcifications, sensorineural hearing loss and hepatosplenomegaly: congenital infection (TORCH), a primary leukodystrophy and a type I interferonopathy (Aicardi-Goutières syndrome). These were recorded as differential considerations, not confirmed diagnoses.

Availability limits: this is a constructed selected-record review. The CMV IgG results in infant and mother, the negative blood and urine PCR, the MRI description and the CSF pterin results were reported at the systemic work-up stage; the exact timing of specimen collection relative to birth and to surgery is not stated in the supplied record. CMV IgM results, CMV testing on saliva or CSF, and audiological details beyond the BERA summary are not reported in the supplied extracts and are unknown, not necessarily normal or unperformed.

Genetic investigations (chromosomal microarray and whole exome sequencing) are documented later in the source record and are withheld from this decision-point packet; their results are not available at the assessed point. Any genetic testing proposed here is a proposed future request, not a documented decision at this stage.

Later treatment, subsequent surgical interventions, hearing aid prescription, systemic immunotherapy and long-term visual outcome are withheld from this packet and must not be assumed.

prepared_template.title: Painful swollen thigh with marked inflammation but no collection
prepared_template.facts:
A woman in her early 60s was admitted from the emergency department after a fall at home due to profound muscle weakness, with a 3-week history of progressive swelling and severe pain in the right thigh. She denied preceding trauma.

Background: uncontrolled type 2 diabetes for almost 10 years with poor reported adherence to twice-daily insulin; sickle cell trait; iron deficiency anaemia. She had recently completed treatment for a diabetic foot ulcer, including a short inpatient admission 7 weeks before the current admission.

Documented microvascular complications: retinopathy and microalbuminuria. Pain was constant and stabbing, rated 7/10 in severity, 10/10 on movement, and progressively limiting mobility.

Examination: vital signs stable, afebrile. The right thigh swelling was firm and tender without erythema or increased skin temperature. Peripheral pulses were palpable bilaterally.

Right lower limb motor power was graded 2/5 on the MRC scale; left lower limb power was 5/5. Pain-limited volitional effort was noted, with pain scores of 10/10 on movement. Sensation in both feet was intact. A left ankle ulcer was stable.

Inflammatory marker: CRP increased to 248 mg/L during admission (timing relative to the imaging below is not separately stated in the available text) and was 185 mg/L on discharge. The article states antibiotics were considered when CRP rose to 248 mg/L but were deferred; infection team review found no source, and she had recently completed antibiotics for suspected osteomyelitis. The elevated CRP was presumed to reflect inflammation rather than infection.

Imaging available at this decision point: X-ray excluded bone fracture; Doppler ultrasonography excluded deep venous thrombosis; musculoskeletal ultrasonography of the thigh excluded abscess formation by demonstrating no focal fluid collection.

Creatine kinase: the source describes only a mildly elevated CK and states this is atypical of inflammatory myositis. No numerical CK value is quoted in the supplied narrative text; the numerical table was not checked for this packet, so the CK magnitude is unreported here.

Recorded differential diagnoses at this stage: DVT, cellulitis, inflammatory myositis, intramuscular abscess, compartment syndrome and diabetic myonecrosis. Cellulitis was argued against by absent erythema and skin warmth despite elevated CRP, and recent completion of a 6-week antibiotic course for suspected osteomyelitis. Compartment syndrome was ruled out on preserved distal neurovascular status and lack of clinical features of raised compartment pressures.

Availability limits: the contrast MRI of the right thigh has not yet been performed or reported at this decision point; its findings, the final diagnostic attribution, subsequent management and outcome are withheld. The exact admission CRP value (before the in-admission rise) is not stated in the supplied text. HbA1c at presentation is reported in the discussion as 118 mmol/mol, consistent with uncontrolled diabetes, but its sampling date relative to admission is not specified.

Proposed next investigation (a proposed request, not a documented decision at this point): MRI with contrast of the right thigh, which the source later lists among the investigations performed and describes as the imaging modality of choice for this presentation.

prepared_template.title: A growing conjunctival lesion after an initially inflammatory biopsy
prepared_template.facts:
A toddler was referred to an ophthalmology department with persistent unilateral conjunctival hyperaemia and progressive thickening of the nasal conjunctiva in the left eye, present for approximately 3 months before referral.

Before referral, the child had been evaluated at another institution and treated empirically with multiple courses of topical corticosteroids, topical antibiotics and antihistamine therapy, without clinical improvement.

Examination at presentation showed localised hyperaemic thickening of the nasal bulbar conjunctiva of the left eye. The remainder of the ocular examination was unremarkable, with no corneal involvement, intraocular abnormalities or impaired ocular motility.

The child was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and normal perinatal course. Medical history was otherwise unremarkable, with no family history of ocular disorders, malignancy or known genetic syndromes.

An incisional biopsy was performed because of persistent lesion progression despite prolonged medical treatment. Histopathology showed an inflammatory infiltrate, predominantly lymphocytes with rare plasma cells, without evidence of neoplastic proliferation.

Despite the initial reassuring histological findings, progressive worsening of the conjunctival lesion was observed over the following months of follow-up.

Approximately 5 months after the biopsy, the patient returned for re-evaluation because of further lesion enlargement. Additional topical corticosteroid therapy was prescribed; no clinical response was observed. The lesion increased in size and extended toward the nasal limbus, prompting surgical intervention.

At initial presentation, the persistent unilateral hyperaemia with focal conjunctival thickening raised suspicion for chronic inflammatory conditions, including allergic conjunctivitis, chronic infectious conjunctivitis and inflammatory pseudotumour. Lack of response to prolonged topical corticosteroids, antibiotics and antihistamines progressively reduced the likelihood of these diagnoses.

Following the first biopsy, which showed only inflammatory infiltrate without evidence of neoplasia, a reactive inflammatory process, nodular fasciitis, remained the leading diagnostic hypothesis as recorded by the authors. This is documented as a provisional working hypothesis at that point, not a confirmed diagnosis.

Continued lesion progression despite treatment and a progressive increase in tissue volume raised concerns regarding an underlying proliferative lesion. No further tissue, immunohistochemical or molecular results are available at this decision point.

Constructed selected-record review: this packet combines data recorded at different times (initial presentation, first biopsy, and the 5-month re-evaluation). No pretreatment baseline time point is documented beyond the approximate 3-month symptom duration. Exact lesion measurements, dates and imaging at this stage are not reported in the available record.

The report does not establish whether the first sample missed an underlying process or whether the lesion's biology changed over time; both possibilities remain open in the source. No mechanism should be assumed retrospectively.

prepared_template.title: Major reconstruction with inherited thrombophilia
prepared_template.facts:
A man in his 20s presented with a right-sided mandibular ameloblastic fibroma. He had previously been scheduled elsewhere for right hemimandibulectomy with vascularised free fibula flap transfer, but that surgery was cancelled when he disclosed congenital protein C deficiency immediately before the procedure. Sequentially staged resection and reconstruction was proposed at two hospitals; due to his strong desire for single-stage reconstruction he was referred to the reporting institution.

Relevant history: prior surgery for a right meniscal injury under general anaesthesia without perioperative thrombotic complication and without special measures. No medications at presentation. Family history: one brother with chronic pulmonary embolism; one sister with multiple DVT events during pregnancy, leading to diagnosis of congenital protein C deficiency and anticoagulant medication. Genetic testing was not performed due to the patient's preference.

Examination: swelling in the right mandibular area; no cervical or intraoral fistula. Orthopantomography showed tumour within the right mandible.

Preoperative blood tests: protein C activity 53% (reference 64%–146%); protein C antigen 42% (reference 70%–150%); prothrombin time 81% (reference 70%); PT-INR 1.0; APTT 32.7 s (reference 24–39 s); D-dimer 0.6 μg (reference 0–1 μg).

Contrast-enhanced CT reported suspected right lower leg DVT. The treatment section states this CT was performed 1 month before surgery, and that lower extremity venous ultrasonography was performed before surgery confirming the absence of apparent DVT. The exact dates and the interval between the CT and the ultrasound are not separately specified; the two results come from different modalities and times and cannot be merged into one contemporaneous result.

The source records that edoxaban 60 mg once daily was started because of the CT-noted lower extremity DVT, and that the patient was admitted 1 week before surgery with continuous intravenous sodium heparin to maintain APTT at 1.5–2.0 times baseline preoperative values. Protein C supplementation was started 5 hours before surgery. These are documented management steps recorded in the treatment section; the preoperative planning record itself does not state who decided them or when the decision was made.

The source records that the diagnosis of protein C deficiency was based solely on family history and protein C activity and antigen levels, because genetic testing was not performed. Protein C supplementation had no target value and was administered at the package-insert-recommended rate. The source also notes the high cost of protein C replacement therapy and that its administration warrants thorough discussion of the financial burden on the patient.

The source states that because the case involved hemimandibulectomy with plans for postoperative extensive jaw bone-supported device implantation, reconstruction methods other than a free fibula flap were not feasible, and that free fibula flap surgery carries a high risk of venous anastomotic thrombosis. The source also notes that the risk of anastomotic thrombosis in head and neck free flaps is reported as 0.8%–10.6%, and that it is unclear whether this risk is higher in protein C deficiency.

The CT report of suspected DVT and the later ultrasound showing no apparent DVT are recorded at different times; the source does not state whether the suspected CT finding was ever formally confirmed or excluded before the ultrasound, nor the exact dates of either.
