prepared_template.title: Haemorrhagic brain lesion years after pregnancy
prepared_template.facts:
Presentation: A multiparous woman in her early 30s, with no known comorbidities, presented to the Emergency Department after three unprovoked generalised tonic-clonic seizures within 2 days. Each seizure involved brief loss of consciousness, bilateral involuntary jerky limb movements, upward eye deviation, hypersalivation and urinary incontinence, followed by 20–30 minutes of postictal confusion. She had no history of epilepsy.

Over the same 2 days she also developed sudden painless bilateral visual loss progressing to complete loss of light perception, acute right-sided limb weakness, diffuse holocranial headache and projectile vomiting. There was no history of fever, recent head trauma or anticoagulant medication.

Reproductive history: Her last menstrual period was about a month before admission. She had two uncomplicated full-term vaginal deliveries. She underwent suction evacuation for a complete hydatidiform mole 5 years ago, after which serial beta-hCG levels returned to normal. A subsequent pregnancy 4 years ago ended in intrauterine foetal death at 35 weeks' gestation; histology of the products of conception at that time showed no trophoblastic abnormalities.

Examination findings: She was conscious but slightly drowsy in the postictal period, afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Neurological examination showed right-sided hemiparesis with motor power 3/5 on the MRC scale, increased tone, brisk deep tendon reflexes and an extensor plantar response in the right limbs; sensation was intact throughout.

Cranial nerve examination showed complete bilateral absence of light perception with slow-reacting pupils, while extraocular movements were completely normal. Funduscopy at admission showed normal optic disc margins with no papilloedema.

Imaging: Emergency non-contrast CT of the brain showed a solitary haemorrhagic lesion in the left occipital lobe, with a central hypodense core, a surrounding hyperdense rim and moderate perilesional vasogenic oedema causing mild sulcal effacement; there was no midline shift. No other intracranial lesions were found. CT venography was unremarkable.

Baseline blood tests showed a normocytic anaemia (haemoglobin 10.4 g/dL) and a normal coagulation profile.

Documented initial working diagnosis (provisional, as recorded at the time): Given the abrupt onset and haemorrhagic appearance on imaging, primary intracerebral haemorrhage was considered early on. However, a well-defined mass lesion with surrounding vasogenic oedema, lack of established vascular risk factors such as hypertension, and the occipital location rather than basal ganglia or thalamus, were noted as arguing against a primary vascular aetiology. Cerebral venous thrombosis was also explored but considered implausible given the isolated well-defined lesion and a completely normal CT venogram.

The imaging findings were also recorded as consistent with a haemorrhagic metastatic lesion. Melanoma, renal cell carcinoma and lung carcinoma were noted as causes of haemorrhagic cerebral deposits, but the patient's young age and lack of systemic symptoms or primary site characteristics made this less likely. Her previous full molar pregnancy drew attention to gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. Infective lesions and primary brain tumours were considered implausible in the absence of fever, immunosuppression or characteristic imaging features. These remain unconfirmed diagnostic considerations, not established diagnoses.

Record availability limits: This is a constructed selected-record review. prepared_template.title: Recurrent delayed postpartum bleeding after reassuring intervals
prepared_template.facts:
A woman in her late 20s, gravida I para I, previously healthy with no medical history, delivered by caesarean section performed for non-reassuring fetal heart rate tracing; the delivery is described as uncomplicated. This record is a constructed selected-record review: the facts below were documented at different assessment times and are presented together for review, not as a single contemporaneous assessment.

First episode (day 26 postpartum): she presented to the emergency department with heavy vaginal bleeding of 1 hour's onset. She was pale, normotensive and normocardic, with moderate active vaginal bleeding on examination. The uterus was anteverted, involuting, mobile and non-tender.

Day-26 investigations: transvaginal ultrasound showed an empty uterine cavity with a 23 mm×24 mm hyperechogenic image at the isthmus, reported as suggestive of a thrombus. Coagulation study was unremarkable; haemoglobin was 111 g/L.

Day-26 management and course: she received 1 g tranexamic acid and 5 units of oxytocin, with resolution of bleeding. Haemoglobin 5 hours later was 86 g/L, haematocrit 0.266 L/L, platelets 276×10⁹/L. She was transfused 1 unit of packed red blood cells and discharged on desogestrel 0.075 mg. At 2-week follow-up she reported no complaints, haemoglobin was 126 g/L, and vaginal ultrasound was unremarkable.

Second episode (day 156): she returned to the emergency department with sudden heavy vaginal bleeding. She was pale, nauseated, afebrile and normotensive. Haemoglobin was 138 g/L, serum β-hCG negative, and coagulation profile (prothrombin time, INR, aPTT) normal.

Day-156 imaging and management: TVUS demonstrated endometrial thickness of 8 mm and a cystic lesion at the uterine isthmus consistent with an isthmocele (47 mm×38 mm) containing hypoechoic material suggestive of blood. Cervical dilatation was performed, evacuating a significant volume of blood with subsequent cessation of bleeding. She was discharged on combined oral contraceptive therapy.

Day-157 deterioration (current decision point): the following day she was admitted to the emergency room haemodynamically unstable, with decreased level of consciousness and profuse vaginal bleeding. Immediate resuscitative measures were undertaken: intravenous fluids, 1 unit of packed red blood cells, 1.5 g tranexamic acid, and uterotonic therapy with 10 units oxytocin and rectal misoprostol 800 µg. No further imaging results, haemoglobin values or subsequent management are available in this record at this point.

Recorded differential considerations at this stage: because the postpartum haemorrhage was delayed, recurrent and unresponsive to conventional management, a broad differential was considered. Retained products of conception were initially considered but imaging did not demonstrate retained intrauterine tissue, making this less likely.

Chronic endometritis was included in the differential; the patient remained afebrile with no additional clinical signs of acute pelvic infection, though chronic endometritis may present with few or no systemic manifestations. Coagulation disorders and gestational trophoblastic disease were also considered, but the normal coagulation profile and negative serum β-hCG made these unlikely. These remain recorded considerations, not confirmed diagnoses.

Availability limits: no Doppler flow assessment of the isthmic lesion, no angiographic imaging, no histology and no post-day-157 laboratory values are available in this record. Unreported information is unknown, not normal. The day-26 ultrasound interpretation (thrombus) and the day-156 interpretation (isthmocele with blood) are documented contemporaneous readings; the record does not state whether Doppler interrogation was performed at either earlier assessment.

prepared_template.title: Fetal haemorrhage and neonatal purpura after a sibling death
prepared_template.facts:
This is a constructed selected-record review of one family. The index patient is the second neonate, assessed at the initial neonatal work-up. Data about the first sibling were acquired at a different, earlier time and were never confirmed; the two records must not be merged into a single confirmed history.

Family history (unconfirmed): the first pregnancy produced a term male neonate who developed purpuric skin lesions within hours of birth, followed by seizures and clinical features suggestive of coagulopathy; he died on the fourth day of life. No coagulation studies, protein C activity, molecular genetic testing or autopsy were available for him, so severe congenital protein C deficiency remains only a clinically suspected diagnosis in that sibling.

Antenatal findings (index pregnancy): routine ultrasonography at 32 weeks' gestation showed bilateral severe ventriculomegaly (right lateral ventricle 18 mm; left lateral ventricle 20 mm) with echogenic intraventricular material suggestive of intraventricular haemorrhage. No associated intracranial structural abnormalities or abnormal Doppler findings were identified. Fetal MRI was not performed.

Birth and early neonatal course: a female neonate weighing 1.8 kg was delivered at 33 weeks by caesarean section for preterm labour with meconium-stained liquor. Apgar scores were 2 and 4. Within 8 hours of birth she developed purpuric lesions over the limbs and trunk, followed by lethargy and apnoea requiring ventilatory support.

Initial coagulation studies: prothrombin time 22.3 s (reference 11.5–15.5 s), INR 1.9, activated partial thromboplastin time 58.6 s (reference 28–45 s). Fibrinogen was reduced at 126 mg/dL (reference 180–400 mg/dL) and D-dimer markedly elevated at 7.8 µg/mL FEU (reference <0.5 µg/mL FEU). Fibrin degradation products were positive, consistent with an ongoing consumptive coagulopathy.

Thrombophilia evaluation: protein C activity was markedly reduced at <1%. Protein S activity (64%) and antithrombin III activity (81%) were within laboratory reference ranges. These findings were recorded as highly suggestive of severe congenital protein C deficiency. No anticoagulation was administered to the newborn.

Cranial ultrasonography on day 2 of life demonstrated massive intracranial haemorrhage with midline shift.

Documented management at this stage: admission to the neonatal intensive care unit immediately after birth. Human protein C concentrate was unavailable at the institution; replacement therapy was initiated with fresh frozen plasma (20 mL/kg intravenously), followed by repeated doses of 10–15 mL/kg every 12 hours. Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, vitamin K, inotropic support, ventilatory support and blood component therapy were administered as clinically indicated. No specific anticoagulant regimen was reported.

Availability limits at this decision point: molecular genetic testing (PROC sequencing) had not yet returned a result in the supplied record, and no genetic confirmation is available at this stage. Investigations for fetal/neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia, congenital infections and detailed evaluation for cerebrovascular malformations are not reported in the record up to this point; their status is unknown, not negative. Parental protein C levels were not obtained.

Background context supplied with the record: fetal intracranial haemorrhage has heterogeneous causes, and congenital protein C deficiency is a rare inherited disorder in which severe biallelic deficiency presents predominantly in the neonatal period with purpura fulminans, disseminated intravascular coagulation and thrombotic complications; cerebral vascular thrombosis and haemorrhagic complications are recognised manifestations of severe disease.

cases.title: Multifocal brain lesions and immune abnormalities during B-cell depletion
cases.summary:
Background and acute course
An adolescent male with established Evans syndrome presented with two weeks of headache, nausea and vomiting, worse at night and in the morning. He reported intermittent left-hand numbness/weakness and diplopia. Initial MRI showed a right frontal white-matter lesion about 4.0 × 3.0 × 3.3 cm, oedema, right lateral-ventricular mass effect and about 7 mm right-to-left midline shift. Three smaller lesions were in the left frontal lobe, corpus callosum and right lateral-ventricular trigone. Enhancement was mild and the dominant lesion had a rim of restricted diffusion.

prepared_template.facts:
Background and acute course
An adolescent male with established Evans syndrome presented with two weeks of headache, nausea and vomiting, worse at night and in the morning. He reported intermittent left-hand numbness/weakness and diplopia. Initial MRI showed a right frontal white-matter lesion about 4.0 × 3.0 × 3.3 cm, oedema, right lateral-ventricular mass effect and about 7 mm right-to-left midline shift. Three smaller lesions were in the left frontal lobe, corpus callosum and right lateral-ventricular trigone. Enhancement was mild and the dominant lesion had a rim of restricted diffusion.

CSF and initial assessment
CSF contained 61 nucleated cells/µL, 98% lymphocytes, with normal protein and glucose. IgG index and synthesis rate were normal, but supernumerary oligoclonal bands were reported. The exact band count and paired-serum pattern are unavailable; CSF restriction cannot be independently confirmed from this summary. MOG-IgG and AQP4-IgG were negative. The documented evaluation for infectious, rheumatological, lymphoproliferative and neoplastic alternatives was described as negative, but its component methods/results are not supplied.

He received intravenous dexamethasone before lumbar puncture, a single IVIG dose of unspecified indication and a documented course of intravenous methylprednisolone. Headache resolved and neurological function improved during admission. Plasma exchange was not documented. Exact calendar dates and age are withheld in the source.

Subsequent neurological record
Follow-up MRI described extensive bilateral cerebral T2/FLAIR hyperintense white-matter abnormalities with T1 hypointensity and no abnormal restricted diffusion. A right frontoparietal enhancing focus measured about 13 × 11 mm and was smaller than on its preceding scan; left periventricular enhancing foci of about 9 mm and 5 mm were also smaller. Some left frontal enhancement resolved. No new lesions or significant hemispheric atrophy were reported; mild posterior callosal atrophy was unchanged. These descriptions do not establish that every later focus is identical to the original dominant lesion. At the selected clinical review, he denied recurrent neurological symptoms; family described stable school performance and examination was stable.

Immune findings and limits
During rituximab exposure, circulating B cells were absent and IgG/IgM reduced. Naive CD4/CD8 proportions and stimulated CD40-ligand/ICOS expression were reduced; direct antiglobulin testing was positive and soluble IL-2 receptor mildly raised. SAP expression and XIAP testing were essentially normal, but a CD19 component could not be reported. Chromosome-breakage/telomere studies were normal; a primary-immunodeficiency panel and whole-exome sequencing did not identify a unifying pathogenic finding. Pretreatment immunoglobulins, exact quantitative trends, timing of all immune tests, detailed infection history and a current complete safety assessment are not supplied. No final diagnostic synthesis, selected maintenance regimen, long-term immunoglobulin replacement plan or later outcome is provided.

prepared_template.title: Recurrent optic symptoms with low-titre antibodies and untreated viral infection
prepared_template.facts:
Background and first episode
A woman in her 60s had stage IIIA right-lower-lobe squamous lung cancer treated with chemotherapy, lobectomy and adjuvant chemotherapy, completed about 18 months before neurological onset. Surveillance has shown no recurrence. Liver-test abnormalities had initially been attributed to chemotherapy.

At month 0 she developed left-sided visual impairment (decimal acuity 0.6). MRI showed left optic-nerve and sheath T2 hyperintensity/enhancement, including posterior intraorbital, canalicular and intracranial segments, sparing the chiasm, with apex-predominant sheath enhancement. There was extensive ethmoid/maxillary, sphenoid and left frontal sinus disease without an enhancing mass or reported fungal features. Intravenous methylprednisolone improved vision; no antibiotics were given. Eleven days later optic-nerve abnormalities persisted along the nerve while sinus changes had markedly regressed.

Longitudinal course
At month 3, a week of band-like T10 dysaesthesia resolved spontaneously. Left visual blurring and an afferent pupillary defect recurred at month 19. Lower-limb dysaesthesia at months 29–31 had normal examination and spinal imaging. At month 35, right-eye acuity decreased to 0.8 with bilateral retinal nerve fibre layer (RNFL) thinning; another methylprednisolone course after lumbar puncture produced marked improvement. At month 38, burning pain, urinary retention, myalgias, episodic tachycardia and weight loss were reported. Examination showed a mild left afferent defect and intention tremor but preserved pinprick, reflexes and strength, with no sensory level or ataxia. At month 41 acuity was 1.0 right and 0.6 left, with left disc pallor/tubular field. The current severity and persistence of each autonomic symptom are not quantified.

Investigations available for review
Fixed cell-based serum assays showed MOG-IgG 1:32 (persistent on repeat, including month 35), borderline CASPR2 1:32 and negative AQP4-IgG. CSF bands matched the serum pattern on repeated assessment. Repeated onconeural-antibody panels were negative. Brain MRI showed non-specific punctate foci; spinal MRI at months 0, 13 and 29 showed degenerative changes only. Orbital MRI at months 6 and 32 showed left optic-nerve atrophy/gliosis without enhancement. PET at months 1 and 41 did not identify active high-grade malignancy. Nerve-conduction studies/EMG were normal; endoscopy and mammography did not identify malignancy.

Right RNFL thickness was 95–96 µm through month 5, 60 µm by month 30 and 56 µm by month 41. Left RNFL was 48 µm at presentation and subsequently 35–38 µm; the exact dates of the latter values are not supplied. No later structural/functional trend is provided.

Pre-immunotherapy screening identified untreated HCV, RNA 7,960,000 copies/mL, genotype 1a. Earlier infection records document HCV in 2017 with biochemical hepatitis. Exact current liver staging, baseline immune/infection safety detail and a definitive interpretation of the antibody overlap are not supplied. Maintenance IVIG had been considered, but no final treatment choice, antiviral response, later serology or later relapse outcome is given.

Presentation
A man in his 70s has an enlarging left anterior chest-wall swelling over about three months and progressively worsening low-back pain over several weeks, limiting mobility. No fever, night sweats or important weight loss is documented. He has no known chronic liver disease, viral hepatitis or plasma-cell disorder. The mass is firm and mildly tender near the fourth intercostal space, without overt chronic-liver signs or significant peripheral lymphadenopathy. A current complete neurological examination, pain score and spinal-stability assessment are not supplied.

Initial tissue findings
An ultrasound-guided chest-wall/rib biopsy showed round-to-oval neoplastic cells with eosinophilic/vacuolated cytoplasm, vesicular or hyperchromatic nuclei, small nucleoli and some perinuclear hof-like appearances. The initial immunostains were CD138-positive and pan-cytokeratin-, STAT6- and MUM1-negative. A limited additional panel showed CD138 positivity in most cells with both kappa and lambda negative. The initial report favoured non-secretory plasmacytoma and recommended correlation; this is a working interpretation, not a definitive lineage established by the supplied tests.

Systemic investigation
Renal/liver tests and corrected calcium were reported as normal apart from a mild ALP rise. HBsAg and anti-HCV were negative. Serum electrophoresis/immunofixation found no monoclonal protein. Kappa and lambda free light chains were both mildly raised, with a ratio of 1.59. Marrow was normocellular with preserved haematopoiesis and about 1% plasma cells, without reported plasma-cell-neoplasm or carcinoma infiltration. AFP was 1.73 IU/mL and CA19-9 was 1.9 U/mL, both within the supplied normal ranges.

Imaging
Earlier cross-sectional chest imaging showed destructive chest-wall/skeletal disease. A dedicated liver-protocol contrast study had not been performed at that stage. Subsequent FDG PET-CT showed a segment-IV hypodense liver lesion 34 × 30 mm, SUVmax 4.5, plus smaller lesions in IVb/VIII; a left adrenal nodule 16 × 15 mm was interpreted as likely metastatic. Lytic metabolically active lesions involved the left iliac bone, L5 and left fourth rib; the rib had a 7.2 × 5.0 cm soft-tissue component. There was no dominant pulmonary lesion, bulky nodal disease or another dominant visceral mass.

Record limits
The images and original tissue slides are not supplied, only reports. No hepatic tissue result, extended lineage panel, PIVKA-II result, final primary-tumour diagnosis or disease-specific treatment/response is provided. The patient’s skeletal pain is current; a later neurological complication must not be invented.

Background
A woman in her 80s has recurrent calcium-oxalate nephrolithiasis and chronic left-renal dysfunction. Eleven years before presentation a renal scan showed left/right differential function 15%/85% with impaired left response to furosemide. A repeat five years later showed 19%/81%, hydronephrosis and delayed response without definite obstruction. These are historical split-function measures, not current global renal function.

Past urine cultures grew MRSA four and nine years earlier, and Proteus six years earlier. Her last documented catheterisation was about three years earlier; no home self-catheterisation is reported. Other history includes hyperparathyroidism after parathyroidectomy, osteoporosis, previous perforated diverticulitis with Hartmann procedure/reversal, remote breast cancer remission, axillary DVT, hypothyroidism, hyperlipidaemia, hypertension and monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance.

Pain course
She reports about two months of progressive positional left-hip/left-lower-quadrant pain, weakness and poor appetite. She denies significant weight loss, fever/chills/night sweats in her symptom history; chronic nocturia is the only reported urinary symptom. At an earlier sports-medicine review, focal trochanteric/sacroiliac tenderness, pain with resisted strength testing, antalgic gait, absence of radicular signs and non-acute radiographs led to a greater-trochanteric-pain label. A six-day methylprednisolone course gave transient improvement; a second was prescribed. Worsening pain and difficulty walking about a week after the second course prompted emergency review.

Current findings and CT
At admission she is hypertensive, tachycardic and febrile, despite the earlier symptom denial; exact vital-sign values are not supplied. She has approximately 15 cm of left-flank warmth/erythema and a raised 5 × 5 × 3 cm costovertebral swelling. She is alert and uncomfortable; abdomen is soft with left-lower-quadrant tenderness.

WBC is 23.2 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin 88 g/L, CRP 239.7 mg/L, ESR 65 mm/hour and albumin 3.1 g/dL. Urinalysis has trace ketones, mild proteinuria and mucus. Two blood-culture sets subsequently show no growth after five days. CT shows a 12 × 10 × 10 cm peripherally enhancing collection extending from the left psoas/retroperitoneum through the posterolateral wall into subcutaneous tissues. The adjacent left kidney has marked cortical thinning and collecting-system dilatation to the mid-ureter without an obstructing calculus. The report raises a destructive chronic renal inflammatory process. The original CT images are not supplied.

Vancomycin/cefazolin were begun for suspected cellulitis and broadened to vancomycin/piperacillin-tazobactam after concern for abscess. The selected record combines the admission imaging with the subsequently available negative blood-culture report; it does not assert that five-day culture results preceded treatment. Current numeric renal function, complete haemodynamic trend, abscess microbiology, definitive renal pathology and operative-risk/preference review are not supplied. A urine culture was not obtained during this admission. No drainage response, nephrectomy decision or later recovery is given.

prepared_template.title: Syncope with captured VT and major outflow-tract compression
prepared_template.facts:
A man in his 70s presented with sudden early morning syncope without prodromal symptoms, no chest pain, palpitations or postictal confusion, and spontaneous recovery within 2 min. He reported two similar episodes over the preceding 3 months. A repeat syncopal event occurred in the emergency department, during which continuous monitoring captured sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT) that terminated spontaneously within 1 min. His history included hypertension for 8 years managed with amlodipine 5 mg daily, with no prior structural heart disease, arrhythmia, connective tissue disease, infective endocarditis, thoracic trauma or cardiac surgery, and no known family history of congenital heart disease, sudden cardiac death or inherited arrhythmia syndromes.

At initial assessment, vital signs were stable (blood pressure 130/84 mm Hg, pulse 82 bpm). Laboratory investigations, including serum electrolytes, thyroid profile and cardiac biomarkers, were within normal limits.

A 12-lead ECG during the syncopal event demonstrated sustained monomorphic VT with inferior axis and left bundle branch block morphology, suggestive of right ventricular outflow tract (RVOT) origin. A baseline ECG in sinus rhythm showed no ectopy and no findings suggestive of early repolarisation, Brugada pattern, conduction abnormality or overt ischaemia.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a giant aneurysmal sac arising predominantly from the right coronary sinus, causing severe compression and nearly obliterating the RVOT. No significant aortic stenosis or clinically relevant aortic regurgitation was identified. Left ventricular systolic function was preserved (62%) without regional wall motion abnormalities or other significant structural abnormalities suggestive of an alternative cardiomyopathic substrate.

CT aortogram demonstrated a right coronary sinus aneurysm measuring 62×48 mm and a left coronary sinus aneurysm measuring 36×35 mm, without rupture, dissection or thrombus. The study was non-ECG gated, resulting in mild motion artefact; however, aneurysm morphology, bilateral involvement and severe RVOT compression were reported as adequately delineated for diagnosis and surgical planning. CT coronary angiography performed prior to surgery demonstrated normal coronary arteries without obstructive coronary artery disease.

During hospitalisation, no premature ventricular complexes or non-sustained VT of similar morphology were documented. Holter monitoring was not performed.

The aneurysm aetiology was recorded as indeterminate. The late clinical presentation and absence of associated congenital abnormalities or a relevant family history raised the possibility of an acquired process; however, in the absence of histopathological confirmation or an identifiable secondary cause, an acquired aetiology could not be established. Histopathological examination findings were unavailable at the time of manuscript revision.

Record availability limits: this is a constructed selected-record review. The CT coronary angiography was performed prior to surgery and therefore later than the initial imaging; no pretreatment ambulatory rhythm recording exists, as Holter monitoring was not performed. The CT aortogram was non-ECG gated with mild motion artefact. Histopathology was not available. The aneurysm subtype (congenital versus acquired) is not established. No data are provided beyond the stated decision point; later management and outcome information is withheld from this packet.

prepared_template.title: Persistent facial palsy and hearing loss after a normal CT report
prepared_template.facts:
A woman in her 50s with a history of stage III left-sided invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast (ER-positive, PR-negative, HER2-negative) was referred to the otolaryngology service with presumed Bell's palsy. She reported progressive left-sided hearing loss and intermittent tinnitus, but denied otorrhoea, vertigo and recent upper respiratory tract infection. She was independent in activities of daily living and had no history of tobacco or alcohol use.

Four years earlier, she had been diagnosed via breast screening with a 30 mm, grade 3 invasive ductal carcinoma with associated ductal carcinoma in situ. Sentinel lymph node biopsy revealed one macrometastasis and one micrometastasis, prompting re-excision and axillary clearance, which showed no further nodal disease. She received adjuvant chemotherapy and completed left breast radiotherapy; endocrine therapy was tamoxifen, later switched to letrozole after tamoxifen-related endometrial polyps were found on biopsy.

Two months before presentation, she developed progressive left-sided hearing loss. She then presented acutely with left lower motor neuron facial paralysis (House-Brackmann grade VI), accompanied by midfacial pain, tinnitus and dysgeusia; the ear was not examined at this time.

In the emergency department, CT of the head and paranasal sinuses was performed for presumed Bell's palsy. Her breast cancer history was not documented on the imaging request, and the scan was initially reported as normal. The general practitioner requested urgent otolaryngology review 20 days after this initial presentation, but clinic assessment did not occur until 55 days after the onset of facial nerve palsy.

At otolaryngology assessment (day 55), examination confirmed complete left-sided facial paralysis with inability to achieve eyelid closure, mild left-sided dysdiadochokinesia and limb incoordination, with a positive Romberg test despite preserved vestibulo-ocular reflexes.

Otoscopy at day 55 revealed erythema and bulging of the pars flaccida, retrotympanic opacification and abnormal scarring, without tympanic membrane perforation or the retraction pockets typical of cholesteatoma.

Pure tone audiometry confirmed asymmetric, mild-to-severe, mixed, predominantly conductive hearing loss on the left, with a 15-30 dB air-bone gap. Tympanometry showed a type B curve, consistent with reduced middle ear compliance.

A retrospective re-read of the initial CT identified opacification in the epitympanic and mastoid region that had not been reported. The source does not establish the exact time of this re-read. This reinterpretation is included in this constructed selected-record review; the original emergency department report stated that the scan was normal.

Given these audiological and otoscopic findings alongside the facial nerve paralysis, urgent CT of the temporal bones and MRI were requested at day 55 to assess for structural or neoplastic disease. These scans had not yet been performed at this decision point.

The ear was not examined at the initial acute presentation. The cancer history was omitted from the initial CT request. A GP request for specialist review was made at day 20, and specialist assessment took place at day 55. The results of subsequent temporal bone imaging, histology, oncology treatment and outcomes are withheld.

This constructed selected-record review combines the earlier records, day-55 specialist findings and retrospective re-read of the initial CT. The exact time at which the re-read became available is not established. Do not treat the re-read as evidence available to the original emergency team or infer that it was available at a specific day-55 decision.

prepared_template.title: Biliary obstruction years after pancreatic drainage
prepared_template.facts:
A woman in her early 70s presented to her local medical practitioner with an acute history of right-sided abdominal pain.

Background history: idiopathic necrotising pancreatitis 3 years earlier, complicated by walled-off necrosis requiring an EUS-guided cystogastrostomy and three necrosectomies through an endoscopically placed 15 mm LAMS. At the final necrosectomy, the LAMS was removed and two pigtail drains were left in situ with no plans for removal.

Follow-up imaging 4 months after the drainage procedure demonstrated resolution of the necrotic collection. On that early scan the stent was positioned near the head of the pancreas and the common bile duct was not dilated.

Other notable history included a splenectomy and breast cancer requiring wide local excision and axillary dissection.

On presentation 3 years after the pancreatitis, ultrasonography and CT of the abdomen demonstrated a common bile duct dilated to 20 mm with a 25 mm distal CBD calculus, without any cholelithiasis. A single pigtail stent remained in situ; the second was presumed to have passed through the alimentary tract, but this was not demonstrated.

On the current CT, the pigtail component was reported as lying within the distal bile duct with a superimposed bile duct calculus and upstream biliary dilatation. The superimposition of the calculus onto the pigtail component was not reported at the time of the original scan.

An attempt at outpatient ERCP was unsuccessful: the guidewire failed to advance beyond the calculus/pigtail complex.

Following the failed ERCP, a referral was made for a cholecystectomy and open bile duct exploration. This is the decision point under review; no operative findings, cholangiography results, stent removal, stone retrieval or subsequent course are available at this stage.

Constructed selected-record review: the device history, the 4-month interval scan and the current imaging were acquired at different times, and the current CT was not originally reported as showing stent/calculus overlap. The passage of the second pigtail was presumed, not confirmed. No pre-referral cholangiography, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography or other anatomical detail beyond the stated imaging is available in this record.

Contrast-enhanced MRI of the right thigh revealed a lobulated intramuscular mass involving the right vastus medialis in the mid-portion, measuring 5.6×4.4×7.7 cm. The lesion was closely related to the superficial femoral vessels medially without encasement; the neurovascular bundle was normally visualised and the femoral cortex intact, with no bone erosion or periosseous abnormality. The mass showed avid post-contrast enhancement with prominent intralesional and peritumoural flow voids.

Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy demonstrated nests of tumour cells forming pseudoalveolar patterns separated by thin sinusoidal vascular spaces, with moderate nuclear pleomorphism and granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. Findings were considered strongly suggestive of alveolar soft part sarcoma (ASPS), with definitive characterisation deferred to the resection specimen. PAS with diastase on the biopsy showed focal intracytoplasmic rod-shaped crystals.

Baseline staging: contrast-enhanced CT of thorax and abdomen demonstrated no distant metastatic disease; a subcentimetric nodule (4.2×6.0 mm) with adjacent fibrotic bands in the left apico-posterior segment was considered non-specific, with interval follow-up advised. Screening brain MRI revealed no intracranial enhancing lesion. Staging followed AJCC 8th edition: greatest dimension 7.7 cm on MRI (cT2) and 6.0 cm on the resection specimen after fixation (pT2); FNCLCC grade 2, N0 and M0, classified as stage IIIA.

The patient underwent wide local excision of the right thigh. Intraoperatively an ill-defined intramuscular mass of approximately 4×7 cm at operative assessment involved the right vastus medialis, displacing the superficial femoral vessels medially without encasement. The previous biopsy tract was incorporated in the excision; feeding and draining vessels were ligated.

The resection specimen measured 13.0×7.0×3.0 cm and contained a tumour of 6.0×4.5×3.5 cm. All margins were microscopically negative: superior 1.2 cm, inferior 1.0 cm, medial 1.2 cm and deep 0.8 cm. The overlying skin was free of tumour. FNCLCC grading yielded grade 2 (total score 4: differentiation 3, mitoses 1 (7–8/10 high-power fields), necrosis 0).

Resection histology showed a partially circumscribed tumour arranged in nests and lobules separated by thick fibrous septa containing a rich capillary network, with central loss of cellular cohesion producing a pseudoalveolar pattern; cells were large, round to polygonal with vesicular nuclei, prominent nucleoli and abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. Immunohistochemistry showed vimentin positivity, with S100, desmin, pan-cytokeratin, CD34 and CD56 all negative. PAS with diastase revealed focal positivity for intracytoplasmic crystals.

The working diagnosis recorded at this point was ASPS, reached on morphological and exclusionary grounds: the characteristic pseudoalveolar architecture, PAS-positive diastase-resistant intracytoplasmic rod-shaped crystals, vimentin positivity and negativity for all other markers tested were considered diagnostic. This remains a provisional diagnosis; the source itself states the limitations of a diagnosis reached without TFE3 confirmation.

Molecular confirmation was not obtained: TFE3 immunohistochemistry was not performed and fluorescence in situ hybridisation for ASPSCR1::TFE3 rearrangement was not available at the treating institution. The source states TFE3 nuclear immunoreactivity is generally regarded as necessary for a definitive diagnosis, given overlap with TFE3-rearranged PEComa and translocation-associated renal cell carcinoma. The panel also did not include melanocytic markers (HMB-45 and Melan-A) or myogenic regulatory proteins, which would have strengthened exclusion of PEComa and alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma respectively.

Differentials were addressed by the exclusionary panel: alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (desmin negative), paraganglioma (CD56 negative; PAS-positive rod-shaped crystals characteristically absent), intramuscular haemangioma/arteriovenous malformation (excluded on core biopsy histology), translocation-associated renal cell carcinoma (no primary renal lesion on staging; pan-cytokeratin negative), granular cell tumour (S100 negative) and undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma (typical age and pattern differ). PEComa exclusion was incomplete because melanocytic markers were not in the panel performed.

The institution reported that inverse-planned IMRT capacity was prioritised for other anatomical sites and was not available for this patient. This is resource context for the constructed review, not evidence that adjuvant radiotherapy was selected. The board recommendation, any treatment-planning actions, delivered technique or dose and later outcomes are withheld.

Explicit availability limits of this packet: the tumour board's recommendation, any radiotherapy actually delivered (dose, technique, fractionation), treatment response, the later status of the non-specific lung nodule, and follow-up beyond the immediate postoperative period are not supplied and must not be assumed. Unreported information is unknown, not normal. The lung nodule is recorded only as non-specific with interval follow-up advised; no benign characterisation is documented at this time point.

Use these five sections:
